Question: How is the Punjabi language different from Hindi and Urdu?

So, within in this greater region itself, on the top we have Dogri, Kangri, Pahadi Languages. On the North West we have Potohari and Hindko, on the South we have Puadhi, Bagri, Haryanvi. On the Southwest we have Saraiki,Derewali.(Not to mention Shahpuri, Janghli, Jatki etc). Many of these are not dialects of Punjabi, or let’s say atleast of Eastern Punjabi. They are their own Languages (though they don’t have official status so it’s hard to gauge their current standing). Anyways, as a Eastern Punjabi speaker, we have these almost dozen other vernaculars or Languages with which we have certain differences which can depend from minor to significant. (Usually dependent on exposure and interest). I have translated a Dogri/Pahari song to Eastern Punjabi but then not many people write 900+ answers on Punjabi over a period of 6–7 years on a forum :) Even within Eastern Punjab, we speak differently amongst ourselves. Thus, comparisons with Hindi/Urdu are way out of scope in this domain as far as finding differences, relatively speaking that is.(as there would be lots).

Question: Are Saraiki, Hindko, and Mirpuri dialects of Punjabi?
Answer: Personally, I dont consider Saraiki, Hindko and Mirpuri as dialects of Punjabi, but let me provide some prespective. Firstly, what I call Punjabi, is Eastern/Standard Punjabi or rather Gurmukhi Punjabi. (90+% of my Punjabi interaction has been with this Group). So, I would classify the vernaculars of lets say North-West Indo Aryan as follows : My rational of demarcating or segregating them is because if any person speaks the 2nd and 3rd category of Languages, they will have to Switch to Standard Punjabi in a deliberate attempt. In Linguistics that would be major change. (I am not talking about Mutual Intelligibilty nor whether they can be mixed or not). Coming to category 1, may be 100 years ago even Eastern Punjabi dialects had more differences but today they have pretty much diluted to a large extent under the ‘Gurmukhi Punjabi’ umbrella, that we dont have to switch our dialects when talking to each other. These 3 Eastern dialects are essentially dying, in lieu making space for Punjabi as that is the natural course. The geographically adjacent area to Eastern Punjab has the closest Language, but the Punjabi Langauge status there is at the lowest situation (Lahore). Now there is ‘transition’ area between Western Majha and Lahnda(Saraiki) in West Punjab, where Jatki/Jhangochi is spoken and that Language is intelligible for Eastern Punjabis with some effort. I have learned and had some interaction that this region still identifies pretty strongly as ‘Punjabi’. Infact, many of the historical Punjabi prose is said to have come form this region and even said to be the real sound of Punjabi. In Summary, at best we can put the languages in a cluster of North-Western Indo-Aryan. They are sometimes called ‘Punjabi Languages’ or Greater Panjabic but I am personally not comfortable with it. Maybe if there was some cohesive history or lineage of Old Punjab/Punjabi from Nath or Baba Farid times, but it doesnt exist. Sure its counter-intutive in ways, as one one hand we call Baba Farid the first major poet of Punjabi but actually he wrote in Multani. This is a senstitive topic, and I never understood the point of imposing an idendity on someone as everyone should have freewill in it. In a way, it is good that these Languages never came under a single umbrella because invariably some would be suppressed in the process, as its just how it is. (may be some of that grievance exists in West Punjab, but we in Eastern Punjab are isolated and thus un-aware of it). My Grandmother was from Sargodha which comes under Lahnda(Shahpuri), but by the time I had conciousness of interactions with Her, She had been in the family for very long time, which was exclusively Doabi, so her native vernacular perhaps had seen a steep decline. Only some of her different vocabulary survived. The Eastern/Gurmukhi Punjabi by default has more usage of Native Prakrit type words plus its also diverging as it uses some sarkari terms and has seen more standardization. The modern Gurmukhi prose also takes on more Sanskrtized terms as needed which takes it further away from the larger Perso-Arabic influences seen in Lahnda. (Native Punjabi has no words for Governmental usage, like ‘Capital’ or ‘Corporation’ and so on, and thus uses loanwords from Sanskirt in the Eastern side).

Question: Why did the Punjabi language lose its significance in the Punjab province?
Answer: We can make an approximate chronological pattern of ‘Prominent Languages’ of Empires which have ruled over the Punjab region across the Last millennia. Ghaznavid dynasty : 977–1186 , Persian (official and court language; lingua franca) , Arabic (theology), Turkic (military) Ghurid dynasty before 786–1215 , Persian (court, literature) Malmuk Dynasty, 1206–1290, Turkic (main) , Persian (administration) Delhi Sultanate , 1206–1526, Persian (official and court language), Hindavi (semi-official between 1451 and 1526) Mughal Empire, 1526–1857, Persian (official and court language), Urdu (later given official status), Hindustani (lingua franca), Chagatai (spoken in the initial years), Arabic (for religious ceremonies) Sikh Empire , 1799–1849 , Court language (Persian), Spoken languages (Punjabi, Saraiki, Hindko, Pothwari - Pahari, Kangri, Dogri). British Punjab/India, 1849–1947, Urdu (Official Language). West Punjab(Pakistan) has continued with Urdu as it’s official Language. Erstwhile Eastern Punjab(Political) has parts which have Hindi and Punjabi as official Languages. If we analyze this trend, we can see that Punjabi never really had a royal patronage for much of its history. So, Punjabi can’t be compared to Languages like Tamil Or Kannada, or even Urdu/Hindi in that respect. (Dogri/Dogra Akkhar did have Royal Patronage in the hilly regions for a period). But thing is that until 100 or so years ago, this didn’t really harm the language that much. Infact, both Persian and Punjabi thrived in the region for almost 1000 years as mentioned in the following article. The reason for this was that the literacy level was way low during those times, so only the elites would learn Persian or later Urdu. So, Punjabi continued as a famous language of prose and daily use during those times. But over the last 100–150 years, when literacy rates and general mass media consumption started going up, Punjabi or other Languages of the region missed the opportunity to position themselves as a viable languages of governance. This is where the real decline of these Languages started in earnest. (Currently, the erosion is more in Urban regions but over generations it will decline in rural regions too). Still, considering the background of Punjab history, the emergence of Gurmukhi Punjabi can be seen as a success. (half dozen or more ‘Native’ scripts of the region have gone extinct). In this respect, Punjab is different from Bengal, which though also divided over Religion, was still able to maintain and secure its common native Language and Script.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Does Punjabi sound pretty or harsh language?
Answer: Personally speaking, we never had any special experience while speaking Punjabi.(Good or Bad). Sure, if someone speaks Punjabi, on a personal level I can connect better as that’s the language I am most comfortable in, but we don’t extrapolate it into making it anything universally significant. (As in even if I feel it’s the language I like the most, I know that’s only for me or us, it means not much to others.) It’s just a Native Language or Mother Tongue for us, just like other people have their own.(which we duly respect). I have always explained non-Punjabi and non-Indians about our native language with no issue. Whenever we had lived as minority, we never thought ourselves as that. We learned the majority languages(for education, jobs, career) and kept speaking our language too among us. We never had a Teacher or Classmate mention anything to us about our Ethnicity or Language even if we were small number of Punjabis/Sikhs in the School. As for the ‘harsh’ part, I am aware that certain perception exists regarding Punjabi as a rural or rustic language, but I think it’s Punjabis themselves who think like that. I have never faced that in our lives. (And I have met perhaps dozen different Indian Ethnicities, no one has mentioned anything negative about Punjabi Language). You can say that I am grateful that we grew up in a environment that neither did we become too proud of being Punjabi nor had any bad experiences, thus it’s just a positive and neutral experience.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Why do most Punjabi and North Indians prefer Roti whereas Bengali prefer rice in their food?
Answer: My thinking was that diet is geographically(and weather) based, and to a large extent, it is true. Bengal does have a favorable climate for Rice production. But, I was corrected one time that Punjab also can and does produce a big amounts of Rice, especially with the agricultural advances of the last few decades. I found the following from the National Geographic Society,[1] which says the same thing. Food staples traditionally depend on what plants are native to a region. However, with improvements in agriculture, food storage, and transportation, some food staples are changing. For example, in the islands of the South Pacific, roots and tubers such as taro are traditional food staples. Since 1970, however, their consumption has fallen. Still, there are differences, we can't say just because Punjabis can grow Rice today, they will start eating it 2-3 times a day and give up on their Allo Paronthas :) I can share some life experiences, as I have exposure to both cultures. Our Mother came from Punjab and learned to make Rice and Bengali food for us.(Since our Father was born in Bengal, Rice had already become our Staple food). She makes one Roti for herself during Lunch along with Rice, while our Father and we brothers just eat Rice for Lunch. (Unless really required, We don’t eat Chappati for Lunch(and almost never at home), it will be an abnormal activity for our taste buds or you can say dietary habits). On the other hand, our Mother says she doesn't feel ‘full’ if she doesn't eat some Roti/Wheat. (Yes, even after 40+ years of marriage, these eating habits have not changed). So, what does Punjab do with the huge amount of Rice crop they produce(called Jhona in Punjabi Language), they export it to the rest of India. And since Punjabis eat Rice relatively sparingly, they usually eat long-grain rice, while regions that eat Rice as a staple food, may have more than a dozen types of Rice varieties. One time I asked our Aunt(Punjabi but living in Rajasthan), and She confirmed that they eat Rice about 2 times a month, but when they came to visit us here in USA, they started eating Rice every day with us :). So, mass transportation and improvements in agriculture techniques may have made all types of staples and grains available in different regions and eating habits may be changing little at a slow rate but still we can’t completely ignore ancestral habits and patterns.

Question: Which is more pathetic of an Indian cricket fan, the 2003 final or the 2023 final?
Answer: Its not even comparable. Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: The Sikh book is written in Punjabi. What does that Punjabi sound like? Is it more like modern Indian Punjabi or Pakistani Punjabi?
Answer: The Sikh Religious book is not written in Punjabi Language, as is usually believed. Neither is the Language used in Guru Granth Sahib mutually intelligible with Modern Punjabi. The languages used include Punjabi and its dialects, Lahnda, regional Prakrits, Apabhramsa, Sanskrit, Hindustani languages (Brajbhasha, Bangru, Awadhi, Old Hindi, Deccani), Bhojpuri, Sindhi, Marathi, Marwari, Bengali, Persian, and Arabic. [1] Neither is the Popular salutation, Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh in Modern Punjabi (because its using Ka/Ki, rather Da/Di). The confusion arisis because Gurmukhi Script is used. In many Gurudwaras you can see both Punjabi and English Translation of Hukumana in Sant Bhasha. So, correct estimation would be to say that Punjabi is Native Language/Mother Tongue of Punjabi Sikhs, Punjabi is not the Liturigical Language of Sikhism, though the Gurmukhi Script indeed is attached to the Religion. (There are other reasons why Modern Punjabi Language got more attached to Sikhism).

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What is the meaning of the Punjabi word 'pindon'?
Answer: Pindon(ਪਿੰਡੋਂ ), is an extension of Pind(ਪਿੰਡ), which means Village. Pindon thus means, ‘from Village’. For example, Pindon Dur BaiThyan Nu Changiyan Laggangiyan Aah Ruhdari Diyan Gallan. Sitting Far Away from the Village You will like these soulful talks. Actually, from my understanding this is an example of Agglutination in Punjabi of Pind+Toon -> Pindon. (As in Hindi it would be ‘Gaon Se’ as two separate words, which can be used in Punjabi too though as ‘Pind Toon’).

Question: Being an Indian, I supported Australia in the finals of the 2023 World Cup as my favorite player was from Australia and I support Australia on a regular basis in cricket. Is that fine?
Answer: Even though I felt little bad for Indian Team in the recent World Cup Loss, that was mostly because they were playing like champions and lost in somewhat of a upset. Question: Do most Sikhs speak Punjabi rather than Hindi or Gurmukhi (the Sikh script)?
Answer: Actually Sikh Gutka’s ie Small Booklets based on Guru Granth Sahib are available in Devanagari script also, since we grew outside Punjab we saw them all the time. Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Is Bollywood film industry actually Punjabi and Urdu film industry?
Answer: Not really, though Urdu and Punjabi do have usage in Bollywood. First thing if we track the ‘box office’ of Bollywood movies, its very easy to see that the penetration of Bollywood movies is pretty weak in most of North India. A Tamil movie can do 175 cr from 7+ cr population, but a Bollywood movie does 500 cr from lets say 70 cr population who can follow or use Hindi Language for media consumption. (Could be even 80–90 cr though). If Hindi Language had same resonance or penetration in North India, a Hindi Language movie should do 1750 cr business but its not even doing one-third that business. Which brings us to the fact that while Bollywood is called Hindi movie industry, the business is pretty fragmanted if we dig down the details. (A Rohit Shetty movie usually does big business in Gujarat/Maharashtra, a Akshay Kumar or Sunny Doel movie historically does big business in Delhi/North, Shahrukh Khan is biggest in West Bengal/Mysore, while a Salman Khan is biggest in CI(Central India) and Rajasthan). That is why you will see Akshay Kumar using a Punjabi song in his movie, while Rohit Shetty will use Marathi touch more. Thus couple of years ago a new term ‘Pan India Movie’ became famous after success of Bahubali and KGF etc, because they were giving some taste of how much business a universally accepted movie can do in India. Coming back to Punjabi, people who speak Punjabi natively can very easily identify that the type of Punjabi used in Bollywood is kind of diluted (which is expected), as even in North India only a small section speaks Punjabi Natively, though more can probably understand it. Recently, a Punjabi song was released from the movie Animal, and very many people are saying that finally ‘Real Punjabi’ is used in Bollywood which it is and surely such Punjabi Language wont be used in the movie as it would be hard to understand for Hindi/Urdu audience. But fact is that this is still a ‘Popular Type’ Punjabi Song just sung in a folk way, and the vocabulary level of this Song is almost to the level of this UK Type Punjabi song (which also mixes some English). So, I think its a combination of couple of things, where firstly ‘what is Punjabi’ has not been fully defined or understood. And also, there is a certain overestimation about what ‘Hindi Industry’ represents via Bollywood. If someone from Patna goes and watches a movie based in Mumbai, ofcourse its going to have a different flavor.

Question: How many letters are in the Punjabi language?

When we learn these words, we make sounds like : Uda, Eda, Eidi, Sassa , Ha-haa ,K-Ka, Kh-Kha , Ga-Gga, Gha-Ga and so on..

Question: Are Bengali and Bangla the same?
Answer: Yes it is the same thing. Bengali is the English pronounciation. Bangla is the Bengali native pronounciation. Different Languages have different words/spellings for same thing. For example : In Punjabi, we call Bengali -> Bangali. (the first e vowel is not stressed). In Bengali, Punjabi is called -> Paanjabi. (the first u vowel becomes long a). In Spanish, English becomes -> Inglés

Answer: Start with Bhalobashi - Like/Love :) Good - Bhalo (My nickname among some of college mates in Punjab when they found out I came from Bengal and wanted to learn some words, so there are some Punjabis who learned this Bengali word from me). Nomoshkar -> Bengali version of Namaskar where S-> Sh and inherent A vowel -> O Dhonnobaad -> Bengali version of Dhanyawaad, Changing Vowel A -> O and W -> to B Sanskrit क्ष (Ksh) is pronounced as Kh, thus Akshay -> Okkhoy in Bengali. Is - Aache (Bhalo Aache , it is good) Me - Ami You - Tumi/Aapni How - Kemon/Kerokom How are you - Tumi/Aapni Kemon Acho/Aachen? I am Good - Ami Bhalo Achi. Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Do Punjabi and Dogri speakers share a common language?
Answer: No. In India, Punjabi(Eastern) and Dogri are considered separate languages. (I also consider them separate languages). We can say they belong to same Bigger Language Family, as in they have the same sound characteristics (Tonal) and largely a shared vocabulary. I would assume one can understand each other (mutually intelligible) for the most part. My Parents lived in Jammu for few years in early 80’s, with my Dad working on a Dam project there and they confirmed that they were able to interact with Dogri speakers without major issues. I think Dogri or a closely related variety is called ‘Pahari’ on the Pakistan side. The variety of Punjabi we speak(upper Doaba) has some sound characteristics more similar to Dogri than the Central Punjabi(Majhi), for example we say Bakh (separate) and Band (distribute) like Dogri rather than Vakh or Vand (like Majhi). One time I had translated a Dogri/Pahari song to Punjabi/English, am sharing a link.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Are Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, Gujarati and Marathi all mutually intelligible? If yes, then why is there a need for English in India?
Answer: No, these languages are not Mutually Intelligible. Here in USA, once I met a Gujarati Gentleman, who could only speak in Gujarati. He couldnt speak Hindi or English. It was interesting experience, starting with English/Hindi, then trying broken Gujarati, couldnt really speak full Punjabi and finally Sign Langauge/Gibberish(we just said whatever we wanted to, expecting other to pick up something). So, we could not understand each other much. We kind of used sign language and it worked out. I can compare it with when I communicate with Spanish speaking people here in Southern California(who cant speak English). Growing up we had Marwadi neighbors, and their Mother could only speak Pure Marwadi and Our Grandmother could only speak Punjabi. Living together for decades, they learned to understand each other (even though Marwadi and Punjabi are not mutually intelligible but then thats how Creoles and Pidgins are created). Neither of them learned Hindi or English.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Do most people in India know Hindi, Tamil and English?
Answer: Actually, Hindi speaking and Tamil speaking are the most monolingual or lets say bilingual people of India(if we include English). Tamil speaking people (~8%) usually dont learn Hindi like rest of Indians do, as second or third language. They are the only people who didnt accept the 3 Language formula in India. (and in effect stopped Hindi from becoming the National language of India, like lets say Urdu is of Pakistan). Indian Government did have plans but they have been hold since 1960’s. This decision of Tamilians also led to increase of English usage in India. Hindi speaking people (~42%) usually dont learn any other regional language. ‘By Book’ they do have option to study other langauges but due to little implementation and thus lack of resources, pretty much everyone just studies Sanskrit as 3rd language. They dont need to learn a regional language because they are already speaking the dominant lingua franca which others will learn to interact with them. This is a normal majority-minority linguistic dynamic the world over. Between them, we have around 50% Indians, who only know their language(or related dialect), plus English if one has studied upto Graduation and beyond (more in Urban areas).

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Are there any Punjabi customs a Punjabi American probably wouldn’t do?
Answer: Any person from Punjabi ancestry who is born in America or West in general, is an American or Western first and foremost. I have met people like these and I have relatives/cousins too. Most of their values and customs are Americanized or Westernized in other words. Some of it depends on family to family also, though. Rest could be a personal quest of their identity, as one grows up, like some may take more interest in their ancestral homeland or others may have no interest. Like, how one of my Cousins told me why people are attaching ‘India/Punjabi’ with him and that he is a English speaking Canadian, which in essense he is. Still there are some remnants of the ancestral culture we can say, most of them seemed to have the same study/work ethic to become productive members of the society. Though, we have to respect the fact that they grew up in a country or west in general which has high emphasis on individuality. I am among the eldest among our group, and I have also always been dealt with mutual respect, can we call it Indian/Punjabi custom or culture, I guess we can but I don’t know. Most cant speak the Ancestral Language with fluency. So, overall it would be more like they are just following some of the ancestral values and culture, but have also moved on to the new identity and culture they were born in, which is all but natural, as their future generations slowly shed their Punjabi or Indian background and become fully American or Canadian.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Are the different Punjabi dialects mutually intelligible?
Answer: My exposure to various dialects of Punjabi while above average still is not huge. It is not that easy to answer but to make it easier what we have in Eastern Punjab (Doabi, Majhi and Malwai) and certain regions of Paudh can be said to be mutually intelligible (also since these dialects do use Punjabi in mass media we end up learning about each others way of speaking also which dilutes the differences over time). And even though I am Doabi speaker , because I spent 4 years in Malwa, Malwai now sounds just like a native level vernacular to my ears. Puadhi is more similar to Punjabi and Bangru is more different. (I can understand many words due to exposure to Haryanvi/MarwaDi). But I can’t understand some words of Bangru. So Ofcourse I can’t speak Bangru and even can’t speak Puadhi, so these can make a case to be ‘different’ enough from what is becoming Standard or Mainstream Eastern Punjabi. In other words, a ‘Standard’ language’ can never cover all the up-Bolis or Dialects of the region and in an ideal world it should be up to the individual if He or She feels inclined to associate with the said Standard Language. (But many a times it doesn’t happen, even worldwide famous languages like French, German, Italian or Spanish engulfed or absorbed many vernacular’s when they were standardized). Since Eastern Punjab is relatively small in area, the variation while there isn’t huge.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: How many Punjabis have Urdu as their mother tongue?
Answer: There is a significant number of Punjabis who don’t speak Punjabi(or Languages of the Greater Historical Region) as their first language or home language. (Ie The language they speak to Parents in). When you meet such Punjabis, invariably you will find out that if they do speak Punjabi, they learned it outside their homes and later in life. (Or dealing with the outside world ie streets and markets). I would estimate 20% or even 30% of people of Punjabi ancestry speak Urdu or Hindi as their home language. Because of lack of education in Punjabi, Punjabi definitely is not their literary language of expression.(even if they show some interest in it as a spoken vernacular). In urban cities with larger Punjabi populations, like Lahore, Delhi, Islamabad, and parts of Haryana. (I am forgetting the name of the city but one time I read a report from one other Larger West Punjab city, that only 3% of Parents wanted their next generation to learn/study Punjabi). Lahore used to be center of Punjabi Language and Culture it is said, but by mid 20th century it was competing with Lukhnow as the hub of Urdu Language, thus Punjabi has almost gone out of the upper/middle class there. Even in some urban areas of Indian Punjab or Chandigarh young generation is speaking Hindi, I have heard. This information may be a little surprising for some as people usually think that a community still continues to speak the Native language at home even if it’s not the official language of Schools and the Government. That is true, but that only happens in the first couple of generations. Since Hindustani/Urdu/Hindi has been the official language of large parts of Greater Punjab for like 5–6 Generations(175+ years), the Punjabi community or society is way past that point linguistically. So unlike usually believed, this inclination of Punjabis towards Hindustani goes way before Partition. (It had already started in earnest around 1850’s onwards). And this phenomenon will only increase in times to come(less in Indian Punjab as Punjabi is an official language there). As an example, We can compare it to Ukrainians, of whom almost 50% speak Russian as Mother Tongue. It’s normal phenomenon for Official/Prestigious (perceived) language to penetrate from Urban to Rural regions over many generations. And ‘Mother Tongue’ can and does change across generations, just like we acquired Punjabi as a Mother Tongue long time ago we can lose it too.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What is the meaning of the Punjabi word “majhail”?
Answer: Majha,ਮਾਝਾ (Punjabi) or Majjha, मज्झ (Pali) is a Indo-Aryan Prakrit word related to Sanskrit Madhya.(मध्य) It means ‘Center’ or ‘Middle’. In Punjab’s case its used to refer to both the Central Region of the Historical Region (covering Amritsar and Lahore) and also the dialect being spoken there. Majhail thus any person coming from that region. In Pali, the use of the word can be seen in Majjhima Nikāya ("Collection of Middle-length Discourses"), a collection of Buddhist Scriptures. Having said that, While the word indeed is retained in Punjabi in the above contexts, it also seems like this is an Archiac word in Punjabi today, because in Modern//Colloquial Punjabi, words like Maddh(ਮੱਧ), Vichkaar and Gabbhe are used for ‘Middle’ or ‘Center’ of something.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What are the differences between American and Australian English?
Answer: Both are huge countries so there is lots of variety in between them but some which I can remember. Australian English uses lots of Vocabulary from Commonwealth(British) English which we study in Countries like India also. Restroom is called Toilet. Cookies are Biscuit. Elevators are Lifts. Garbage Bin can be Litter, Rubbish or Garbage Bin. Freeway could be Motorway(Sydney) or Freeway(Melbourne). Regular(Black) Coffee is called Long Black with Milk. (And Flat white is the opposite). From my understanding American English doesn’t have any equivalent of ‘Mate’. The vowel ‘A’ is almost spoken as ‘Ai’ , thus Space becomes Spaice. You see brands like Caltex and Dulux which we saw growing up in India. We knew of all major Australian cities and how Australians generally speak just by watching cricket. Hungry Jacks is the Australian Burger King. Because we got UK type English Education in India growing up, learning Australian English would have been bit easier, but we have already learned American English now, so Australian English just gives glimples of what we learned or used back in India. But at the end of day it’s just English. Anyone from English speaking country would be comfortable in couple of months (especially if one has lived around a metropolis where we hear variety of accents/vocabulary anyways).

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Why did the Sikhs reject Sanskrit when it was clearly a language that could be used to communicate complex religious ideas (like writing)?
Answer: I have read few answers on a similar topic which tend to agree with the premise of the question. But of course this is not true. If one has spend some time reading passages of Guru Granth Sahib, it becomes clear there is Sanskrit being used. Now sure, Persian was also a language of high culture back then and thus it was also used along with many other languages of the region used by common people. Gurū Nānak’s poetic language also incorporates a quite high proportion of Perso-Arabic loans, amounting to an approximate total of 700, as against 1,500 Sanskritic items and 3,600 New Indo-Aryan words (Shackle 1984, p. 77). [1] New Indo-Aryan here would mean what can be called Old Hindi (Braj) or Old Punjabi. Sikhs even today majorly use Sanskrit or say New Indo-Aryan(Prakrit) based first names(in few cases mixing with Persian words). Modern Punjabi(main language of Sikhs) is usually considered as being descended from Sanskrit, even in dictionaries/books written by Sikhs. Even if one goes with the logic that modern Punjabi developed separately and in parallel with Sanskrit as an ‘Prakrit’, still it behooves a person to learn some Sanskrit if one wants to know source of very many Punjabi words. Reason being there are not many books or literature showing this gradual formation of modern Indo-Aryan language, while Sanskrit literature is abundant. Moreover, the modern Eastern Gurmukhi Punjabi language whose development was also mostly led by Sikhs, is also ironically at times said to be Sanskritising Punjabi. (Compared to say the Punjabi Language of 19th Century, which had lots of Persian flavor as was majorly propagated by Punjabi Muslims). Thing is languages which have never been themselves used in official capacity before always have to use loanwords from languages which were in high culture historically, which personally is fine for me as any day I would be comfortable saying the word for ‘State Capital’ as Rajdhani(Sanskrit) rather than Dar-Ul Hukumat(Persian). Sure Sikhism and Buddhism(Theravada) don’t use Sanskrit as Liturgical Language like Hinduism but whether one learns or uses Punjabi,Pali or Sant Bhasha all are inevitably related or connected to Sanskrit. Any one learning those languages deeply would eventually learn decent level of Sanskrit too. Within our immediate family, we have names like Mohan, Kulwant, Kartar, Tej, Ganga, Gian and so on. Sure, some are not crisp Modern Sanskrit names like Hindus but all are indeed rooted in Old Prakrit, Indo-Aryan and Sanskrit base.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Do the people of Punjab speak their own language called ‘Punjabi’ or do they only speak Hindi with a different accent?
Answer: While it is true that the Hindustani language by now has a long history and influence in ‘Punjab’ and on Punjabis(it has had an uninterrupted run of 175+ years in the region), just like it has on regions like Rajasthan, Bihar, Haryana, Jammu and Himachal(and Pakistan), I would still say that the differences between the pronunciation of Hindi and Punjabi are more pronounced than compared to MarwaDi, Bhojpuri or Haryanvi. It is possible that these other vernaculars earlier had major differences also but have already reached a diluted stage that mixing Hindi with them has become easier. (For example, I read a document about the historical similarities between Bhojpuri and Bengali as both belong to the Magadhi Prakrit Lineage, but today Bhojpuri is considered more closer to Hindi as its the official langauge there[1]). In real life , at least from the Indian side Punjabis usually speak Punjabi and Hindi as separate languages. There are almost 40–50% different words so if one’s Punjabi is decent it’s hard to mix the languages. (at least I can’t). On the other hand, I have heard of ‘Gulabi Punjabi’, a diluted version of Punjabi spoken on the Pakistani Side by mixing it with the Hindustani variant of Urdu. And that is also the reason West Punjab has more skill in mixing Urdu with Punjabi. (because they use Urdu as the language of Education and Office). My parents sometimes watch those Pakistani shows where the host speaks in Urdu and the comedians make jokes in Punjabi, there is lot of linguistic intermixing going in that environment. In same way, the languages of Hindi Official regions have indeed become dialects of Hindi, as people of these regions are mixing their native vernaculars in a major way with Hindi, and the demarcation between the two is diminishing. So, it’s not like Punjabi can’t reach the diluted stage of Bhojpuri or MarwaDi but currently, it’s holding a bit better linguistically that it’s usually considered a separate language rather than a dialect or accent of Hindi. (it also helps that Punjabi has a separate script and official usage in the Eastern Indian Punjab side).

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Is Punjabi a tonal language like Chinese or Vietnamese? If so, how many tones does it have?
Answer: Yes Punjabi is a Tonal Language like Chinese and Vietnamese but the level of tonality is less. Others and I have also written answers on this topic but today I will give only specific examples related to H(ਹ) sound in Punjabi. For example, the following 3 words are pronounced almost similarly in colloquial Punjabi. (I am sharing because these came to my mind on their own, and later I did some study on them). ਨਹੁੰ -> Means Nail or Finger Nail ਨੂੰਹ -> Means Son’s Wife or Daughter in Law (When ੂ/ uː/ comes before ਹ/ɦə/ , the sound sound of first syllable is extended to second).[1] ਨੌਂ -> Means the number 9 All 3 are pronounced as Nau. When we say Nau-Katla(cut your nails), Nau-Sass da Rishta (Daughter in Law-Mother in Law Relationship), or Nau Baj Gaye (it’s 9 o’clock), the Nau is similar sounding. Since Gurmukhi doesn’t have special tonal markers in the written form H(ਹ) can be seen. Literally speaking H sound can be made in the middle or end of a word but naturally speaking Punjabi(or the ancestral language doesn’t). It just shows the ancestry of the word. It can be seen akin to Sanskrit loanwords in Thai where the loan letters are written even if the pronunciation is in the Thai way. For someone like me, who with no Punjabi Education started writing Punjabi later in life(after the age of 30), many a times finding the word in Dictionary took a while (because how it’s spoken and written can be different). We write ‘outside’ as Bahar but say ‘Baar’. We write ‘a lot’ as Bahut but say ‘Baut’. We write ‘no’ as Nahi but say ‘Nai’. And very many more, this is because of Tonal Nature of H(ਹ) in Punjabi.(depending on the location). I am posting some excerpts and you are read in more detail in these links.[2] [3]

Question: How can I learn the Doabi Punjabi dialect?
Answer: Doabi Punjabi is a very popular variety of Punjabi Language, so if you have been listening to Punjabi media for a while(which is today dominated by Indian/Eastern version), you are unknowingly already exposed to Doabi Punjabi in a major way. You can follow some rules if you know Standard Punjabi or other flavours of Punjabi.(Majha/Malwa) Kivien/Kinj/Kistran -> Kiddan Jivien/Jistran -> Jiddan Einj/Estran -> Eiddan Try to finish sentences with ‘Aa or Ya’ for almost every situation. (which in Standard Punjabi we write as ‘Hai’ or ‘Haan’). Or end sentences with Siga/Sigey. Tu Kiddan Ya or Tussi Kiddan Ya. Standard Punjabi = Doabi Punjabi. Han = Ya Haan/Hai = Ya/Aa San = Sigey/Si. Vekho = Dekho Usage of B/Bh instead of V/W(though at times it’s a soft B/Bh sound). WaaL = BaaL(Hair) Vaar = Baar(Times) Vi = Bi(Also) Viah = Biah(Marriage) Wadda = Bhadda(Big) Wich = Bech(Inside) Vohti = Bauti(Wife) Wadd = Bhadd(To cut/separate) WanD = BanD(to distribute) Vaisakhi = Basakhi(Festival) Wadhayi = Badhayi (Congrats) I found some information on Degruyter, [1] But it’s not like we can’t speak V/W sound or don’t use it, we do in many words like Wall(Towards), Wang(Type). Sentence example: In Standard Punjabi if we write, ‘How are you?’, it is : Tussi Kiven Ho? But when will speak Doabi Punjabi it more like : Tussi Kiddan Haige Ya? Ofcourse there is lots of regional vocabulary and Aakhan too, like Ghabbe(In between) rather than Vichkaar, Dhaun instead of Gardan(Neck), Niana(kid) and very many others. I have also learned that Doabi doesn’t use R and has other variations, for example. Mundri is Mundi (Finger Ring) , Jindra is Jinda(Lock). Gheyo is Ghe (Clarified Butter), Peyo is Pe (Father). Some regions of Doaba(like upper Doaba from where my Mother is), add H sound in front of A/E in some words, like Haithey instead of Eithey(here), or Haidher(there) instead of Eidher, Hajey(right now) instead of Ajey. Still, Doabi is not that different from Central or Standard Punjabi, infact due to early NRI media it was a famous dialect of mass media. All Major Punjabi Newspapers, All India Radio(Punjabi), DD Punjabi all are in Doaba(Jalandhar). As per my Aunt who was a teacher in Punjab, in some aspects ‘Standard Punjabi’ of Indian Punjab is closer to Doabi than Majhi. One time I read a comment that while historically Majhi was the central or prestige dialect of Punjabi but in the last few decades Doabi became the famous international lingua franca dialect of Punjabi.(It didn’t help that one half Majha moved towards Urdu over the last century). If you want to hear Doabi Punjabi, you can listen to Sangtar and Manmohan Waris. Ofcourse, as ‘Standard Punjabi’ becomes a unified Language on the Indian/Eastern side of Punjab, in times to come the dialects or up-bolis like Doabi will decline and be submerged in it. Its just a natural progression of languages.

Question: What do Sikhs think of the caste system?
Answer: Not all Sikhs grow up in the Punjabi society and thus can be oblivious to the prevailing caste system hierarchy. We grew up in North Eastern region and thus did not build a caste based identity. (Our previous generation was also born there so it was the same for them). We thought you are a Sikh if you look like one(as that’s how others community would see us generally). Later in life we found out about all the castes and clans of Punjabi society. Now, reflecting back and ‘re-constructing’ the history, most of the Sikhs in the North East were non-land owning. (and thus lower on the caste hierarchy). One of our uncle told us a funny story. One time he was talking to a Bengali person in the neighborhood and somehow the issue came up and the Bengali person asked our Uncle ‘Aapni Ki Choto Jaat’, (আপনি কি ছোট জাত). In Bengali Language this means ‘do you belong to the lower caste’. Our Uncle was baffled as he had no clue what was being talked about. Later he found that one of the Higher Caste Sikh had told the Bengali person about our Family’s background ie Caste. In Summary, as I said since we didn’t or couldn’t build a caste based identity, we don’t really have any major viewpoint on it. We know it exists but it’s more like an alien concept. (Sometimes we hear about it from Mother as She is from Punjab).

Question: Is Christianity growing in Punjab?
Answer: Christianity has a long history in Punjab. The first Christian Chapel was made in Lahore, Punjab in 1595 during the Portuguese period when Jesuit missionaries were attending the court of the Mughal Empire. There were three Jesuit missions to Mughal court, as invited by Emperor Akbar (1556-1605). [1] [2] [3] It was closed on orders of Jehangir in 1612, opened again in 1632 but eventually demolished on orders of Shah-Jehan in 1632. Its spread started in earnest in 1834 in Punjab. So, we can’t say the spread of Christianity just started in Punjab. As an observation, using the Native Language of the Land for propagation is a long-standing tradition in Christianity, which is why even if they are a small minority one can find more Bible/Christian-themed resources in the Punjabi language than one can find in Quran/Islamic resources in Punjabi Language(even though Muslims are majority Punjabis by a gigantic margin). On the other hand, a large number of Punjabis like me have been leaving Punjab to live in Christian-majority/based countries like the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. (In our case, our education was also in a Christian School). For someone like me, who you can say is more interested in Punjabi Langauge, I always enjoy Christian themed media made in Punjabi Language. It provides a further dimension to the Punjabi Language. I will say Yes, Christianity is increasing in Punjab. (Eastern side).

Question: How do I promote Punjabi among Punjabi’s so that they can prefer speaking and writing in Punjabi over English, like parents prefer English medium schools and think Punjabi is inferior? How do I change it?
Answer: I think it depends on the family and also upbringing/environment, etc. (As our life experiences are different/individualistic, we can’t club all ‘Punjabis’ together). I can share our family experiences and If I go by our life experience and reasoning, learning other languages and going to an English Medium school can’t be a reason to think of Punjabi as an inferior language. (or the only reason). My Father/Uncles went to study in one of the Elite English Boarding Schools of North East India, Goethals Memorial in Kurseong. So, they studied under actual Britishers called ‘Christian Brothers’ in the lineage of the Belgian Archbishop. (other day our Father showed us his daily diary from his schooling days which he wrote in 1971 in English Language and his grammar, diction , handwriting is way better than us brothers). We also studied at a English School built up by British Priest Father John. (Essentially a Mission - Boys Town). We also had British teachers on Occasions. When I went to Jalandhar in later years, I saw a whole room full of English novels, literature, vinyl music records and player collected by my Father. Their life experiences rubbed onto us too and we also grew up in this somewhat Anglophone environment, watching old Hollywood movies with our Father and listening to English songs since childhood. As much as I write about Punjabi Language, my favorite music is also from English Language bands like Eagles, Bee Gees, Beatles and Dire Straits. It’s possible that one may not learn their native language properly due to various life situations and that is fine, I have many relatives like that, but it’s something entirely different when one thinks those languages are inferior or rural(Pendu in Punjabi) languages. (which needs further introspection as to where that thought process came from). So, in our case, our previous generation(Paternal) has better command over the English language than us and we can never learn or have a relationship with the English language as they do. Just that our ancestors showed us that it is possible to learn other Languages(for School, Jobs, and Business) and still speak Punjabi as a natural native language.

Question: Why do native speakers of certain tonal languages seem to be unaware of the tones in their language? I have asked friends who are native speakers of Punjabi and Samburu if pitch changes the meaning of a word in their language and they said no.
Answer: In the case of Punjabi, its pretty simple. 80–85% of Punjabis dont study or learn the Language in Schools in any form. Even if certain section is able to speak, majority cant read/write the Language, so they have less knowledge about how the language works. The ones like me, who speak Punjabi natively but didnt have education in it (because of being born in a different region), do catch up to the fact that Punjabi is a tonal language after spending time to learn more about the language, because thats how we had been speaking it all along. (And when I showed my Father these differences he also agreed as he also doesnt have education in Punjabi). He even told me how Punjabi actor Dara Singh always used the Punjabi ਘ kàggā [kə̀gːaː] even when trying to speak Hindi/Urdu. Langauges like Mandarin Chinese or Thai are highly documented and have widescale publishing/modern Governmental and Educational usage, that even non-speakers and foreigners with cursory interest know that they are Tonal Languages (they are also more Tonal than Punjabi).

Question: The Tamil language came from the Tamil people, the Punjabi language came from the Punjabi people and the Marathi language came from the Marathi people. Considering there's no Hindi people or ethnic group where did the Hindi language come from?
Answer: There is indeed a ‘Hindi’ or rather ‘Hindustani’ Ethnic group. This is their historical or ancestral region.[1] This common confusion arises because in India, along with Hindustani speaking people , large percentage of UP, Bihar, Punjab, Rajasthan , Pahadi, Haryana etc regions have ‘accepted’ or ‘adopted’ Hindi as their official or first/native language. In the same way, the Hindustani speaking people who went to Pakistan during partition from this region, along with other ethnic people created the ‘Urdu’ Ethnic identity in Pakistan (Karachi). In Pakistan also, large amount of Punjabis adopted Hindustani as their official or representative language. This is also the reason while the original population of actual Hindustani speaking people is estimated to be around 75 million, more than 400–500 million speak it as their first or native language today. Over generations people even start forgetting their actual languages and might start identifying with the new Nation-State/Acquired Language. (Or think their ancestral Language is just a dialect/accent of the Official Language). This may create a point of view that the instituted official Language came out of thin air(and many conspiracy theories), but Ofcourse each Language has its origin/region and associated history. This is a common phenomenon in the creation of new ‘Nation-States’.

Question: Can you learn Punjabi in a week’s time?
Answer: I can share my life experience. I am 39 years old and I probably took a ‘semi-serious’ interest in learning Punjabi around 6–7 years ago. Today it feels odd to even write that I didnt really have much interest in Punjabi Language atleast for first 25 years of my life, but thats for some other time. So, as I understand there can be different phases of learning a language. I had an advantage in that I was already speaking Punjabi as a Native Language or Mother Tongue, with my Grandparents, Parents, Brothers/Siblings and extended family since Childhood. So, I didn’t have to learn how to speak Punjabi. Also had cursory knowledge of Gurmukhi Script coming from Sikh Background. Even if with all these advantages, but lacking academic education, I spent many years and today I am at a decent level of Punjabi knowledge. I have translated few dozen pages from English to Punjabi. I have knowledge of 3 Dialects of Eastern Punjabi. Though I have superficial/cursory knowledge of Hindko, Potohari,Puadhi, Dogri and Saraiki also. Most of our family is from the Doaba region of Eastern Punjab but my Paternal Grandmother was from Sargodha(Shahpuri), and infact I grew up with her in my formative years, away from my parents and my first memories of life/speaking Punjabi are with her only, so I dont know how much that has impact on my spoken vernacular. I still read and write Punjabi slowly compared to say English, so nothing beats academic study of a Language especially in the formative age. As we go across life, many times it becomes harder to make time for such things. Long story short, you cant learn Punjabi or any language in one week :) , but also that its never too late to start learning.

Question: What is the meaning of "Majha" in the Punjabi language?
Answer: ਮਾਝਾ Majha is the Central Region of Punjab. The dialect spoken there is called Majhi Punjabi and historically has been accorded as the most prominent dialect because the region has 2 most important cities of historical Punjab, Lahore and Amritsar. Even though it’s generally considered the Standard dialect but when spoken in its pure form and flair it is not a neutral dialect and has very many different peculiarities which make it stand apart. (For example Saada(ours) of Standard Punjabi becomes -> Haada sometimes, Assi becomes Ahhi and many more). Some other famous characteristics are using ‘Deya’, Karan-Deya, Vekhan-Deya', and the usage of ‘Han/San’ and Je at the end of sentences. The first part is generally not used in written form of Punjabi but second part is used in Standard Punjabi. Another one I learned from college mates from Majha was the usage of the word, ‘Bhau’, ਭਾਊ as a Nick Name or ‘Brother’. One time I read a comment that today only people in rural areas speak like that. But that just means that the more neutral kind of Punjabi is taking over, as It’s inevitable that all dialects will eventually phase out and merge into the Standard form of the language. (In a region where education in the Standard is provided). While speaking Doabi style in our family, we had Majhi speaking family living just across house in Bengal so we had this exposure from childhood and being exposed to Punjabi Mass Media it was relatively straight forward to learn written Punjabi (with some Majha touch). I have indeed picked up a lot of Majhi and Malwai later life too after interaction and living among them.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What are some words that only Punjabis would understand? What makes them unique to Punjabis?
Answer: Punjabi is not a encryped Language. Its open to anyone and everyone to learn and speak. I know of atleast one Non-Punjabi who speaks fluent Punjabi with us. So, in that sense, just like any other Language, there is nothing specific or unique about Punjabi Language. Having said that, personal habits and traits of individuals do linger over a lifetime. For example, I remember when we 3 brothers were kids, we used to speak Punjabi so fast/uniquely that other Punjabis around us sometimes used to tell us to slow down as they wouldnt understand what we were saying. That aspect went away as we grew up, but no one speaks ‘Standard or Literary’ Punjabi in real life, we all carry our ancestral dialects/vocabulary in our speech from where we came from or were born (especially if one is born outside Punjab). Another example, we may still say amongst ourselves, ‘BaDi Bech Anaar Da Gaach Siga’ , that is our own version of Punjabi/Creole. In Standard Punjabi, I guess that would be, ‘Bagiche Wich Anaar Da Rukh Si’. Here, Wich -> Bech, Si -> Siga are aspects of Doabi Version of Punjabi. Gaach is the Bengali word for Tree. At other times, I have caught myself(or say our Father) using Nepali/Bengali equivalent words instead of Punjabi too. (We never learned those Punjabi words in our formative years). My Paternal Grandmother, who essentially could only speak Punjabi, created her own creole language when trying to speak to Non-Punjabis/Non-Indians.

Question: Is Bengali closer to Sanskrit than Hindi?
Answer: It does feel like Bengali is Closer to Sanskrit than Hindi. Keeping the borrowed Sanskrit vocabulary aside, as I suppose Bengali can also be made as Shudh as Shudh Hindi, some of the Grammer of Sanskrit seems to be closer or similar to Bengali. For example, The Fish is in Water मत्स्यः जले अस्ति in Sanskrit. (Matsya Jale Asti) মাছ জলে আছে in Bengali (Maach Jole Aache) Having decent knowledge of Bengali, it was straight forward to learn this aspect of Sanskrit of adding or extending a word by E for ‘In/Into’. In Hindi or Punjabi, we have to add a extra word like Mein or Wich for this. But in Bengali and Sanskrit , Jal just becomes Jale/Jole.

Question: How do you say this in English from Bangla "Asha kori amader khoma sundor dristite dekhben"?
Answer: Asha Kori Amader Khoma Ke Shunder Drishtite Dhekben. I hope you will see our apology in good light. In Hindi Same line : Asha Karta Hoon Ki Hamari Kshama Ko Sunder Drishti Mein Dhekenge. Some Notes : Bengali is Gender neutral so the line can be spoken by either male or female, but in Hindi you have to write Karta/Karti. Kshama is a Sanskrit loanword in Hindi, but becomes Khoma in Bengali, the inherent consonant sound being O instead of A, and Ks -> Kh. Like famous Bollywood star Akshay is called, Akkhoy in Bengali. Sunder -> Shundor, Bengali makes Sh sounds rather than S.

Question: In the Punjabi folk song Chitta Kukkad Banere Te, what does this line mean - 'Heera lakh sava lakh da ae, Teeyan waliyan diya rab izzta rakhda ae'? Specifically what does 'teeyan waliyan' mean?

The Punjabi letter here is, ਧ (Dh -> is phonetically written as tà ->tàddā -> [t̪ə̀d̪ːaː]). It is a Tonal sound and to the uninitiated may sound as soft T (just like how many think of Punjabi Bh (ਭ) as P). Dheeyan Waaliyan Diya Rabb Izzatan Rakhda Ae God will Reward Respect to Parents of Daughters.

Question: How much or what percentage can the average Hindi speaker understand Sanskrit?
Answer: Understanding Sanskrit is somewhat hard for average speaker of Modern Indo-Aryan Languages. Other than vocabulary, Sanskrit grammar is also different. I am giving a very simple example, Six girls and five boys were playing. Hindi : छह लड़कियाँ और पाँच लड़के खेल रहे थे Sanskrit: षट् बालिकाः पञ्च बालकाः च क्रीडन्ति स्म Here the Ch(च) represents the And(Aur or Ate) of Hindi or Punjabi. But it’s location is after and not in between. Such and other Grammatical differences will throw off modern language speakers and it makes speaking the language harder too. Similar differences we can see in Latin -> Italian too.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What is the meaning of Agam in Punjabi?
Answer: Agam (ਅਗਮ) is a Sanskrit based Loanword in the Punjabi Language, usually seen in literature. It means Unapproachable or Unattainable. Agam (अगम्).—adj., f. yā, unaccessible, unapproachable, unattainable.[1] Example from Guru Granth Sahib, ਅਗਮ ਨਿਗਮ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਦਿਖਾਇਆ[2] What was not accessed (by doing) Vedas(Nigam), Satguru has shown. Agam is a Sanskrit compound consisting of the terms a and gam (गम्). The gam (गम्) is the Root for the famous Pali/Sanskrit word गच्छति (Gacchati)/गच्छामि Gacchami, which means ‘to go’. buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ ɡacchāmi I go to the Buddha as a refuge.[3] Eventually, the modern usage of ‘Gaya’ in Punjabi/Hindi ie ‘went’ is also related.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: How similar are Spanish and Portuguese? Are they mutually intelligible?
Answer: Even though I dont know either language but I can share a interaction which I recently saw/heard between a Spanish and Portuguese speaker here in USA. At the Irvine Amtrak Train station sometimes we see International visitors who dont know English at all. So I was at the waiting room, waiting for my Train, when I heard the Security Officer say ‘What Language do you speak?’ , and the answer was ‘Portuguese’ (with the understanding that the visitor cant understand English). That is when I started paying attention. The Security officer started speaking some English, then moved to full Spanish. Or then would start with Spanish and speak some English. The visitor would speak Portuguese with some English/Math terms. (they were talking about Train and Times). Finally, they figured it out. And in the End I heard the Security Officer appologize that She could not speak to the Visitor in her Language. They said greetings to each other and moved on. So, overall from what I saw, It was not a comfortable conversation as far as understading each other, and much of what was interacted/interpreted would have been accomplished by just sign language or hand gestures or pointing at Train Brochure. (well may be it was bit better than that). (From my memory, I remember having such converstations with Japanese, Kazakh, Gujarati or Spanish speaking people who couldnt speak/understand much English). Thus, from my small sample size and understanding, I would say that Spanish and Portuguese are not really mutually intelligible. The people who find more similarities in Languages from same lingusitic family actually have already taken time and interest in learning some words/vocabulary of the other Language. That may cloud their judgement onto how even languages with high lexical similarties can sound pretty different, especially if there is no previous exposure.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What is the meaning of the Punjabi word Biba meas?
Answer: The word Biba has 2 meanings in Punjabi. 1 . Biba : Young Woman or Girl (here the usage is strictly feminine). 2. Biba : Gentle and Well-Behaved, but in this case it’s for male usage. Ie Biba Munda. Question: What percentage of Hindi and Punjabi words share the same meaning?
Answer: Around 50–60% of Punjabi and Hindi words have same roots. (This ratio is approximately same for all North/North East-West Indo Aryan Languages.) Having said that, the number of words which are pronounced exactly same between Punjabi and Hindi is like 10% or even less. I can give few quick example. Easier Common root words. I am Hungry. Hindi : Mujhe Bhook Lagi Hai Punjabi : Mainu Bhukkh Laggi Aa/Ae Here only Bhook became Bhukkh (also bit different Bh sound) and Lagi became Laggi. Rest Mujhe as Mainu and Hai -> Aa. (Hai is used in Punjabi but only in literature but not in spoken form). Some words in this category are : Doodh (Milk) -> Dhudh Jhooth (lie) -> Jhuth These words may be somewhat easier to understand though speaking them correctly is different matter. Next comes bit more deviation like: Chahta Hoon -> Chahunda Haan (I want) Loonga -> Lawanga (will take) Or Raakhi -> RakhRi (Raksha Bandhan) (Here we can see some similarities in root words especially in written form, but it’s going to be very hard to speak these Punjabi words for the uninitiated person and when spoken fast they may not even understand them properly). Third category is completely different vocabulary (which is around 40–50% of the words). I want to talk to you. Hindi : Mujhe Aapse Baat Karni Hai. Punjabi : Main Tuhade Naal Gall Karni Ya. Only people who fully know Punjabi would be able to follow this type of sentences. So, depending on the exposure/interest or the type of Punjabi one hears, we get different responses as far as mutual intelligibility. Some say they can somewhat follow what’s being said in Punjabi but then others completely get lost and can’t understand much. Another thing which I think is happening due to mass media, is that atleast people in North India are getting to know Punjabi words like Kudi, Munda, Changa, Sohni etc as they are so widely used in songs etc. But they are not Hindi words, as the equivalent Hindi words are Ladki, Ladka, Theek, Sunder etc. Any person who has learned these and many other words, due to interest or exposure, just knows Punjabi somewhat better, it doesn’t mean the languages are similar or easier to learn. It’s even extreme from the other side when Punjabis say Hindi/Urdu is easy to learn (but Ofcourse they have been hearing/studying it from childhood almost like a Native Language). One only understands the differences more when these languages are learned in isolation. (For example a Punjabi or Gujarati growing up in America/Canada will have harder time understanding/speaking Hindi compared anyone growing up in North India and thus will find the languages more distinct.)

Indeed, we lived in a mixed environment with Bengalis, Nepalis, Tribals and Marwadis. The Marwadis just like us had been living in Bengal for so long that some of them have even become Bengali first-language speakers. So, I learned Bengali not only from Bengalis but also Marwadis. This is because my Dad and Uncle studied and worked in Kurseong and Darjeeling too(both of which are Nepali-speaking regions). The majority of our nostalgia and family discussions still revolve around the Dooars regions of Northern Bengal, ie the foothills of the Himalayas. Question: When did Punjabi script (written) divided into Gurumaki and Arabic style?
Answer: Punjabi Script never got ‘split’ or ‘divided’. Punjabi is an Indo-Aryan Language and the region comes under the ‘Brahmi’ script region, or rather the Sharada branch which was used to write Kashmiri Language and Sanskrit Language in the region as shown below.[1] The region covering the historical Sharada Script. The chart showing link between Gurmukhi/Punjabi and Brahmi Script.[2] The Punjabi Language is said to be become a separate language around 1000 AD, before that perhaps the variety of language was called by other names. Proto-Gurmukhi script has attested history from 1470 AD, but Brahmi Script goes back to 3rd Century BC.[3] The Gurmukhī script is generally believed to have roots in the Proto-Sinaitic alphabet by way of the Brahmi script, which developed further into the Northwestern group (Sharada, or Śāradā, and its descendants, including Landa and Takri).[4] That means these Landa script systems existed in the region before it was called Punjab or the Language was called Punjabi. (We can call the languages Proto-Punjabi or Prakrits). Brahmi Script inscription dated 250 BC in Sarnath.[5] The Perso-Arabic script probably became more popular in the Punjab region after the 11 Century AD. Persian was the main language of administration and culture from the time of the Ghaznavid invasions of the eleventh century until its replacement by Urdu following the British conquest of the Punjab in the 1840s.[6] So, both systems of writing have parallel history in the region. One is Native and One came from Arab region.

Question: Which of these languages (Bengali, Gujarati, Punjabi, Marathi or Odia) is easiest for a native Hindi speaker to learn?
Answer: All of them would be equally hard for a Native Hindi speaker. I am more aware of Hindi, Punjabi and Bengali , so can give some examples. If you want to say ‘Like Him’, Hindi : Us-Ke Jaisa, Punjabi : Oh-De Warga, Bengali : O-r Moton If you want to say , ‘Do you have it?’ Hindi : Kya Aapke Paas Hai ? Bengali : Ki Aapnar Kache Ache ? Punjabi : Ki TuhaDe Kol Haiga ? Bring that thing here. Hindi : Woh Cheez Yahaan Le Aao Bengali : Oi Jinish-ta Eikhane Niye Aao Come Sit Beside me. Bengali : Aamar Kache Aeshe Bose Jao. Hindi : Mere Paas Aake Baith Jao. I will take this. Hindi : Main Yeh Loonga. Bengali : Aami Eta Nibo. Punjabi : Main Aha Lawanga. Spoken Hindustani has straight Persian loanwords, Punjabi has more ‘deformed’ versions of Sanskrit and Arabic/Persian words, while Bengali has straight Sanskrit loanwords but with modified pronounciations. Sanskrit word for Salt, Lavan becomes Lobon in Bengali, and LooN in Punjabi but in Hindi its the Persian Namak. Way too many differences in these Languages to be mutually intelligible. (I have used basic sentences). As someone who knows both Hindi and Punjabi at Native level, Gujarati was almost incomprehensible to me for the longest time(the actual fast spoken language between people). Just recently I have started grasping it a bit better, after years and years of interactions with Gujaratis and hearing the language consistently. (Granted I never put much effort to learn the language, other than greetings and some words). From the little comparison I have done about the lexical similarity between North Indian Indo-Aryan languages vs European languages, they are further apart than say Spanish-Portuguese-Italian. (North Indian Languages have Lexical similarities around 60%, while for these Romance European languages it’s 80+%). Marathi as I had mentioned, sometimes I can understand the gist but other times it’s so different that my mind doesn’t even register it as a Indo-Aryan Language. I heard the popular Marathi song Zingaat and understood nothing. (Same way, Sindhi and Kashmiri people have told me that they dont understand anything in Punjabi songs). Reiterating, these North-Indian Standardized Languages are more different from each other than many European Languages which have their own Nations. Today, the geographical region which uses Hindi as official language is huge, so wherever the region touches these other languages, the people living there (or if Hindi speakers go to work or study in these other regions), due to exposure or interest they may find that specific language closer to Hindi, not due to any inherent closeness. And since these other ‘Regional’ language speaking people learn Hindi as 2nd/3rd Language in Schools and have huge exposure due to mass media, many of them themselves start thinking Hindi is close to these Languages. (This is a normal occurance linguistic hierarchy between Lingua Franca/Regional languages).

Question: Why do many Hindu Punjabis (living outside Punjab) don't speak Punjabi in their homes?
Answer: Very many from these communities left what is today's Pakistan and mostly spread across Northern India, Haryana, and cities like Delhi and Mumbai. It's estimated that as many Punjabis live outside the Indian State of Punjab as inside it. The newer generations have grown up without Punjabi(or other languages of the Greater region like Hindko/Saraiki) education or even a general Punjabi-speaking environment around them. Another important thing that is not usually brought up is that Script is also an issue for Non-Sikh Punjabis living outside Punjab. Gurmukhi still has some element of being seen as a ‘Sikh’ script. One time a Sindhi Hindu shared a picture of the Bhagwad Gita written in Gurmukhi in Ulhasnagar and I have seen Hanuman Chalisa written in Gurmukhi, but such instances are rare and hard to find. I read in a Book about a South Indian visiting Delhi and he encountered a Punjabi Hindu, who when asked about his native language, said that while they speak Punjabi they write in the Hindi Language because Punjabi doesn't have a script. (Something similar to Punjabi Muslims who even if speak Punjabi usually write in Urdu, Hindi/Urdu here means Hindustani language, not just the script). Actually there were almost half dozen Lande scripts which were used by ancestral Hindus and even some Muslims of North India/Punjab in older times, Gurmukhi is just one of the standardized and surviving version. And since Punjabi written in Devanagari or Perso-Arabic doesn't have a stronghold, then the next generation just moves to Hindi/Urdu. (with Sanskrit and Arabic being their liturgical languages). Gurmukhi, I still don't think is seen as a fully unifying Script for Punjabi even in India, as let's say Bengali, Odia or Gujarati is. There is a Religious angle in there also, a Sikh ancestrally from Potohar or Multan may be fine with merging into ‘Gurmukhi/Standard Punjabi’ in their next generation because of Religious solidarity but Non-Sikhs may not and thus incline towards Hindi, which by now has its own history in Greater Punjab region along with Urdu. On the other hand, Sikhs have the benefit of Gurmukhi being attached to their Religion, so for example, within our family itself, we have an example of many relatives living outside Punjab for 3–4 Generations , but still being able to read Gurmukhi up to a decent level without any formal education or government support.(I am not claiming all Sikhs living outside Punjab speak Punjabi, some have moved to Hindi/Other State Language indeed, but certain link with Gurmukhi/Punjabi is in higher ratio among them). Since we already have a head-start on the tool(ie Script), to put into words what we speak, it becomes easier for Sikhs even if they take interest in Punjabi Language later in life. This is Akin to Sindhis in Pakistan who were able to secure their separate script(Rasm-Ul-Khat), and that is why their linguistic adherence is way stronger than Punjabi Muslims(who dont have a proper script to write Punjabi in). But as the question mentions, this is specific to outside the state of Indian Punjab, inside the state everyone speaks Punjabi regardless of Religion as its the state official language (atleast from my experience). I would be interested to know how Non-Sikh Punjabis living outside Punjab view the Gurmukhi script, or in general(I know within Punjab, Devanagari is used in Hinduism).

Question: Why Indian Punjab divided further into three states?
Answer: The current state of Indian Punjab was organized to position Punjabi as the official state language.(to be written in Gurmukhi script). After partition East Punjab was classified as a bi-lingual state (Punjabi and Hindi), which makes no sense as Hindi isn’t even native to the region, but then ‘United Punjab’ earlier had Urdu as the official language(so linguistically things were messed up anyways and the status quo continues in West Punjab/Pakistan today, but let’s not digress). While the move is often seen as divisive as these things usually are, in the long term it has served its purpose well, as Punjabi written in Gurmukhi is a successful and widely used language today, not just in India but overseas too (I am currently visiting Canada and I see the script written on streets and signboards), while other scripts and languages of the greater region have been declining or have even gone extinct over the last 175+ years or so(the time since Hindustani has been the dominant socio political lingua franca of the Greater Punjab region). I am not claiming that Gurmukhi Script or what we call Eastern Punjabi today(Majhi, Doabi, Malwai, Paudhi) are the ‘representative’ script/language of the Greater region for there are or have been other Languages and Scripts in the Greater region too but the fact that those have been discarded or not promoted and hence left languishing towards obscurity means that it was a correct decision to separate a variety of Punjabi which can be used in official usage.

Question: What does the Punjabi word "shae" mean? I've heard it many times before in different sentences like "Tinu kon shae dinda?" Or "prawa ena lokan nu shae lab jandi aah thora jeya has k Gaal kr lawao tae!"

So, that is why Punjabi is called a Tonal Language.

Question: Can every Indian understand the Punjabi language?
Answer: Punjabi is a North Western Language of the Indian Subcontinent, also it is a very large region if we consider the historical or greater Punjab. So, it actually touches Sindhi, Pashto, Kashmiri, and Haryanvi, Rajasthani-speaking regions at its extremities. Thus people who live around those areas would know or understand that closer variety or dialect or in some cases Separate language related to Punjabi. (what is actually ‘Punjabi’ is also not well defined outside Indian Punjab where it is getting standardized now). Having said that, Punjabi is not at a level of a lingua franca, even at a regional level. That is no or very small percentage of non-ethnic Punjabi know or speak Punjabi as an inter-ethnic language like say Hindi/Urdu is. Punjabi never reached that level of a breakthrough as a language. So, we usually talk in Hindi or English with non-Punjabis and speak Punjabi only with Punjabi people.(Thus we never could know how much Punjabi a non-Punjabi would understand). Gurmukhi script is from a different strand of scripts(Sarada) from Devanagari so it’s also not much understood/intelligible. Considering all this and the fact that Punjabis are 3–4% of Indians, I would guess 5% of Indians can understand spoken Punjabi and only around 2–3% can read/write Gurmukhi. (I think even many Punjabis living outside Indian Punjab can’t read Gurmukhi). Speaking Punjabi though is exponentially harder for a non-native speaker(as it happens with any language). On a Personal level, in my whole life of almost 40 years, I know of only 1 Non-Punjabi who can speak Fluent Punjabi.

Question: What is the word for "tea" in Punjabi?
Answer: The word for ‘Tea’ is written as Chah, ਚਾਹ. But spoken Punjabi treats the H,ਹ letter in a tonal way. So we end up saying just Cha. Other examples, Reha -> Rea Nahi -> Nai (No) Sah -> Sa (Breath) Banh -> Ban (Arm) Bahut -> Baut (a lot) Sometimes if H is in middle of the word, it’s changes the words in different ways. Seher -> Shair (City) Sahura -> Saura (Father in Law) There is nothing wrong if the H is pronounced just that then it becomes bookish or literary Punjabi. Coming back, Cha(Tea) has almost the same pronunciation as Cha (which means desire, Eagerness or glee, the shortened version of Chau). Thus we can say in Punjabi, Mainu Cha Peen Da Baut Cha A I am very eager to drink Tea :)

Question: What is the Official language of Bihar?

In our CBSE school located in adjacent Northern Bengal, all Hindi and Sanskrit teachers were either from Bihar or trained there and all had great Pedigree in these Languages. Question: Is Haryanvi a dialect of Hindi or of Punjabi?
Answer: Haryanvi is not a dialect of Punjabi. I understand the similarity in some vocabulary given the proximity and overlapping vernaculars from interaction on the border regions like Bagri, Puadhi or Baazigar Languages, and I am aware of the dialect continuum context. But I don't agree with the dialect continuum talks when they go overboard, as in putting the whole landmass from Sindh to Bengal in same category. (A region perhaps as wide as Europe). That is not how languages are developed and nurtured, we need to come up with borders and carve the similar enough vernaculars under a Standard umbrella as needed (just like we use Gurmukhi to write Standard Punjabi in India).

Question: Is Khatri a type of Kshatriya or Punjabi?
Answer: Khattri(ਖੱਤਰੀ/खत्तरी) is the Punjabi pronunciation of Sanskrit Kshatriya.(क्षत्रिय). Punjabi doesn’t have the Ksha(क्ष) sound of Sanskrit which becomes Kh(ਖ/ख) and also it doesn’t have consonant clusters like Tra (त्र), the T and R are thus pronounced separately. The Sanskrit क्ष in this case has an almost silent K but in Punjabi Kh is pronounced. There is a consonant gemination to T, thus we stretch it’s sound. Thus the transformation from Kshatriya -> Khattri. Khattri thus just represents Punjabi Kshatriya Community.

Question: How is Urdu different from Punjabi?
Answer: Usually, Punjabi Vocabulary is around 50% different from Urdu but sometimes Punjabi can be 90–100% different from Urdu. For example : Assi Oh Utthon Kadhya Siga. (P) Humnien Woh Wahan Se Nikala Tha. (U) We had taken it out from there. There seems to be small grammatical difference too in the sentence but I can’t explain it. In this case Assi is used for Hum/We, but in the next example, Saanu is used. Humien Zaroorat Hai(U) Saanu LoD Ya (P)(we can’t say Assi here). We are in need. Saade-Toon Jarya Nai Jana (P) Humse Saha Nahi Jayega (U) We can’t bear it. So, We have 3 different Punjabi words for extensions of Hum of Urdu/Hindi. Humnien -> Assi/Assan Humein -> Saanu Hum-Se -> Saade-Toon Urdu/Hindi are also more ‘Standardized’ than Punjabi because they have more official support/usage. There are regional varieties of Punjabi have agglutinative type properties like: Saade-Toon -> Saathon The Standard word for ‘Yours’, Tuhada becomes Thoda and even Soda. In Majhi, Saade(Ours) can become Haade. In regions of Doaba, Eithey(here), Ajey(right now) becomes Hiethey and Hajey. Eddan->Einj->Evien->Estran, all means ‘like this’. Then we say, Eh De Wich(in this) as E’che. This is not even slang, just normal spoken parlance. When we speak Punjabi we don’t stop or analyze, most of us know or are exposed to these variations of Punjabi and we just use our preferred ways, with no issue. Then there are Punjabi Sayings or Aakhans, which are at times so different they have nothing in common with Hindustani Language. Saanu Godde Godde Cha ChaDeya (Said when some very good event has happened and is a moment of happiness). I have watched many Punjabi <-> Hindi/Urdu videos and the languages are way more different than I used to think even couple of years ago. As I watched some videos even I got surprised how the words got modified and the difference in vocabulary. Because I know both languages pretty decently, the small modifications which I used to think are not significant are actually pretty big for those who don’t know Punjabi. As far as pronunciation, the pronunciation of words is 90% different between Punjabi and Urdu(even if the root is the same). To my mind(or any Punjabi who knows Hindi/Urdu), ‘Want it’, Chahta Hoon may feel similar to Chahuanda Haan of Punjabi, but for an uninitiated person the difference is bigger. The reason I can appreciate it more now is because lately I have had lots of exposure of Gujarati, and the same thing happens between Hindi->Gujarati, on paper the words may seem somewhat similar due to common roots, but when spoken in daily life, they take a different form due to pronunciation.

Question: Do Indian Punjabis eat Punjabi food like butter masala and tandoori chicken at home every day?
Answer: Not at all. I have read that these creamy/tandoori type Punjabi food actually has influence from Persian/Afghani type of food(aka Mughlai), which todays ‘Indian Punjabis’ brought with them from the Western side of Punjab/NWFP post partition. They did change the base ingredients and added more masala/spice to the local liking.[1] You will mostly find these types of food in Punjabi restaurants and functions/weddings etc. My Mother is from the Eastern side of Punjab and is actually vegetarian, so 90–95% of our home food is also vegetarian. 5% is meat based as my Dad grew up in the Northeast, and that also mostly in the last few years as he developed an interest in making food. I also have lived a few years in rural Punjab(both Doaba and Malwa) and meat is rarely made at home. People get shocked when they see Punjabi meat eating percentage at the level of Gujarat and Rajasthan, but it will be clear to anyone who has spent some time in rural Punjab that it is true. Regular Indian Punjabi home food is thus very plain Dals(Lentils), Allo Gobhi, Rajma, Kadhi, Chote and Wadde Chole, Various types of Saags, Matar Paneer, Allo Paronthe and so on. So, we come to this weird conundrum that what is widely perceived as ‘Punjabi Food’ worldwide is not really eaten on a regular basis by Punjabis(Indian) themselves. Many Indian restaurants here in the US actually are Punjabi, and I explain the same thing to my colleagues that we don’t really eat this food every day at home. I am not saying we don’t enjoy it, just that we eat all these types of tandoori/creamy food sparsely. Once in a while, you run into a Punjabi family, where the host is a real food connoisseur and has an interest in making foods like these at home, but that is so unlikely that one remembers each instance. In Summary we can probably divide Indian Punjabi food in 3 types, first is the normal plain home food, next is some type of creamy/tandoori food(but vegetarian only, this is called Vaishno Food in Punjab, ie Dal Makhani, Shahi Paneer etc which can be found all over Indian Punjab markets), third is the one mentioned in the question. (Butter Chicken, Tandoori Chicken etc).
