Question: Why is Indian Bengal called West Bengal, but Indian Punjab is just called Punjab?

Question: What is the difference between Gurmukhi and Devanagari? Why is Gurmukhi considered more difficult to read and write for non-Punjabis?
Answer: Actually Gurmukhi is easier to read than Devanagari and Eastern Nagari scripts like Bengali/Assamese. This is because of general lack of consonant clusters in Punjabi Language and thus Gurmukhi by extension. A Consonant cluster is created when you merge two different consonants to create a new sound. Languages like Hindi and Bengali have a long list of such sounds (because of Sanskrit Loanwords). It is said there can be more than 1000 combinations of these. A Pure Punjabi speaker can’t speak most of these sounds(or atleast they are not part of Original Punjabi Language). In Punjabi Language these sounds are pronounced separately and thus are easier to read. Devanagari Consonant Clusters example, [1] Bengali Consonant Clusters examples, [2] Couple of example, Vriksh(Tree) वृक्ष becomes Brikho বৃক্ষ in Bengali but Birkh ਬਿਰਖ in Punjabi. Even if we can’t read any of the scripts, it’s clear which one will be easier to read. Even my Surname , Flora can be written more correctly in Bengali ফ্লোরা than in Punjabi, where it becomes Falora, ਫਲੋਰਾ. There are couple of signs in Punjabi for these loanwords but their usage is also in decline, as they weren’t really part of original language sound. You can read more about Punjabi Language pronunciations in Punjabi-Hindi kosh, [3] It say: ‘In Punjabi the usage of these half sound words is slowly on the decline and in their place full words are being used which is in line with the Nature of the Punjabi Language.’ On the other hand, Punjabi has huge usage of consonant gemination(difference here being it’s the same consonant), as in stretching the Consonant sounds, but in Gurmukhi a special diacritic called Adhak is used, ੱ. For example, ‘to tell’, Dass is written as ਦੱਸ in Gurmukhi but in Devanagari it will be written as दस्स. So even here Gurmukhi can be written in a compact way.

Question: What are the differences between Lahnda (Western) and Panjabi (Eastern) Punjabi dialects?
Answer: I guess it depends on the specific region as the Greater or Historical Punjab region is huge in size.(with area and population bigger than many countries). My Paternal Grandmother was from Sargodha(which comes under the Lahnda vernacular of ‘Shahpuri’). In fact, since I grew up with my Grandmother for a few years in my childhood away from my parents, my first life memories are with my Grandmother and for many years I used to think my Grandmother was my Mother. So, of course, I never had any issue understanding my Grandmother(and her extended family) and talked with her with no problem. My Mother speaks Hoshairpuri Doabi(Pure Village style), and My Dad’s side speaks Jalandhari Doabi (somewhat mixed with many languages). My Language thus is a mix of all of the above. With decent exposure to Malwai Punjabi, where I studied for Higher education later in Life. Met many Majhi-speaking students there and here in the USA from Lahore too. I have exposure to Malwai variety of Ganganagar, Rajasthan also as I have many family members from that region also here in the USA. (They also mention that Bagri is also spoken there, and most people are bilingual there). These are mostly ‘Central’ or Eastern’ dialects of Punjabi. My experience with dialects of Punjabi is thus mostly limited to the above only. (My Parents do have exposure and experience of interacting with Dogri speakers because my Dad worked for couple of years in Jammu in the early 80’s). I think if we go way Up and South like Hindko, Saraiki, and Dogri etc, that's when differences become bigger, and they even qualify as separate languages. I have been watching a Punjabi comedy channel which seems to be based in Malwa region and listening to them brought back memories of how the language is spoken there, for example Bhagai Mari Janda, means ‘just talking with no substance’ or ‘Wag Ja’ means to ‘go away’, which is called ‘Nass Ja’ in Majhi and we say ‘Nath Ja’, so there are many differences in Indian Eastern side itself. As per my Mother in older times people rarely ventured outside of their subregions or what we call Up-Bhasha or dialects today. But due to advances in literacy, transportation and mass media, these dialects are mixing with each other, especially on the Eastern side where Standardized Punjabi is used as official language of Governance and Education. In the video below you can see an Indian Punjabi family discussing how they had issues understanding each other within Doabi and Majhi.(both belong to Eastern Punjab). I am still learning more about the vernacular my Mother speaks. Only in the last few days I saw a video about Doabi, that within Doabi there are variations as in some places Eithe(here) is spoken as Hiethe, and Ajey(right now) is spoken as Hajey, and that is how my Mother speaks. (Replacing A/E by H).

Question: Do Indian Punjabis gel better with Pakistani Punjabis than Gujaratis, South Indians or Bengalis when they live in abroad like UK, Canada or USA?
Answer: It depends on where the ‘Indian Punjabi’ is coming from. Not all of us have the same family histories and ancestries. I have lived my life amongst various kinds of ethnicities of the Indian subcontinent. I have spent considerable time among Punjabi(Indian), Bengali, Gujarati, Nepali, MarwaDi(Rajasthani), Bihari, South Indian(Telugu and Tamil), Delhiites, and Himachali. Some I grew up with in childhood, some I studied with, some taught us, some I work with and some are relatives. We even had many Indigenous/Adivasi friends in school (called the ‘Tea Tribes’ of North Bengal/Assam). Our School founded by British Father John, was essentially built around a Christian Mission ‘Boys Town’ followed majorly by the Tribals. So, our concept of any kind of strong ‘Punjabiat’ got diluted over the years and generations. We even lost most of our caste/clan consciousness within Punjabis. I only have a superficial knowledge of Punjab Socio-Politics, I learn some history here and there but my general interest is less. I do follow the Punjabi Language, so with regards to it if I interact with Pakistani Punjabis in any capacity and they show interest in Punjabi, is also welcome and enjoyable, but I can't relate to it in any stronger way on Ethnic lines. (at least in any perceptible way). I am aware sensibilities or interests of people can change as life goes on. I don't live around lots of Punjabis here, but even if I was in Punjabi dominated overseas region like Brampton, I don't think my thinking would change. (we are individuals also after all). In Summary, My Indianess is perhaps stronger than my Punjabiness, though I am not really Proud of either.

Question: Where did you learn Punjabi?
Answer: Well, I have no memories of learning Punjabi nor did I learn it later in life. That is I acquired Punjabi as a Native language during the pre-verbal stages. I have no education in Punjabi, Our home dialect is more of Doabi but I spent a few years in Rural Malwai speaking Punjab with no problem. My earliest life memories are of living with my Grandmother(who was from Sargodha) with whom I lived for a couple of my formative years away from my Parents, and I have memories of my Grandmother speaking in Punjabi. Having said that, if I compare my Punjabi with my Mother/Grandmother or Cousins from Punjab it’s a little diluted though not a lot. For example, I don’t say Buha, Bari, Tarke, Tarkalan/Aathan, KhanD, or GanDe but rather Darwaza, Sware, Shaam, KhiDki, Chini, and Piyaaz. The latter words are also in the Punjabi dictionary but most are loanwords esp Persian.(I assume they came into Punjabi like English words are today). Plus we have some Bengali and Nepali loanwords usage which we brothers and our Dad’s side use more amongst ourselves. (And our Mother also understands). We eat Bengali food also so we call food items by their regional terms we learned, we can’t change that now. So, it is Potul for us and not Parmal/Parwal, and so on. On the other hand, since I did spend some years in Village/Rural Punjab area(plus most years during vacations) and even visited/worked in the fields as one of our Uncles had some agricultural land, I know of some Farming related Punjabi parlance too, like Patthe Waddna(cut the crops), Jhona(Paddy), Kamad(Sugarcane), Majjh Su Pai(Buffalo giving birth/lactation period), Madhani(utensil to churn butter), Sua(a small river or aqueduct) and many others. So, the vocabulary is a little mixed and diluted in some areas but rich in other terms. I have been writing Punjabi for many years now, so I can write ‘Standard Punjabi’ decently. (Even with some Majha flavor though we don’t speak like that). The spoken language just shows our ancestry, where we came from and grew up and that is fine. Punjabi is the only language I can talk to my Mother in, I have done some experiments to see if I can speak other languages and I could not :) As for the Gurmukhi script, we had a Gurudwara adjacent to our House in Bengal, so we have been seeing that script since childhood. And just learnt it on our own(being from Sikh background), most of our family knows it like that. So, not as good as someone who has grown up in Punjab and has had an education in Punjabi but overall pretty good situation and I am improving.

Question: What is the difference between Khatri and Jatt Sikhs? Why do they speak different Punjabi languages?
Answer: Differences in Linguistic or Dialect speech are due to region and not Caste/Clan. For example, our Maternal Ancestral Village is Mundian Jattan, and as the name signifies it’s around 90% Jatt dominated.(of Mundi surname). But us few other non-Jatt Sikhs and Hindus speak the same language/dialect as the Jatts of that Region(in this case Doabi). Another reason, which I have learned is that the Khatris and Jatts didn’t ‘integrate’ with each other that much. What I have learned is that the Khatris who came to Eastern Punjab Side from the West Punjab/Lehnda region after partition were relatively well off(not all, and if not money wise they had good knowledge of business acumen, as they were running many businesses in the Western side of Punjab). So, there was this certain Cold War-type rivalry between these incoming Khatri’s(who spoke the Western Punjab dialects) and the already established Jatt clans of Eastern Punjab. This is where they started pointing out differences in their way of speaking, culture, etc. That is why eventually most of the Khatris actually settled outside Eastern Punjab in places like Delhi and other parts of Northern India and even Metros like Mumbai. If Jatts and Khatris had more interaction then eventually their speech would also intermix a bit more. I am not saying Western Punjab didn’t have Jatts, or that Khatris don’t live in Eastern Punjab. Or that the various Clans within Sikhism don’t get along, they do generally speaking but these are just our deeper human tribal traits that separate us from each other or we can say these are our deep-seated survival inclinations.(the act of living amongs one’s own people, that is why even today Sikhs keep relationships mostly within their ancestral clans/castes). Jatts and Khatris are indeed the top Races/Clans/Castes within Sikhism today. So, these are just dialects of a wider historical region which is a normal phenomenon. If you go to towns of Malwa region like Sangrur, Barnala or Bhatinda, everyone regardless of their Religion or Sub-Caste speaks the same language.

Question: What is the English translation of the Punjabi phrase ‘Jithe tera aunjal likhe ia hai?’ It loosely means, ‘where your next meal is written at’. What is ‘aunjal’? Thank you?

Ofcourse these words are not used in daily parlance regularly, but are definitely part of Punjabi Language. (Can be said to be of literary usage). The said sentence, Jithe Tera Ann-Jal likhya Hai, loosely can be translated to, ‘where life takes you or where life leads you’. Where one’s livelihood or life circumstances takes one. The usage of the word ‘Lekhya’ or rather Lekha is also of prominence. (Something which has already been written). As it means the figurative usage to undergo consequences of what’s has already been decided for one based on past action(Karma). Ie Lekha Dena. (ਲੇਖਾ ਦੇਣਾ). Thus there is an element of pre-determinism also here in the statement.

Question: What is the relation between Punjabi and Dogri languages?
Answer: Punjabi and Dogri are classified as Separate languages in India. But Punjabi has many dialects, and even within these sub-regions, there are some subtle differences. Our Punjabi dialect, from our Mother's side, is Doabi and more specifically Hoshairpur-based (Village Bhulowal/Mundian Jattan). This region of Upper Doaba is closer to Amb/Una of Himachal region than it is to Majha of Amritsar/Lahore. (as can be seen from the image below). For example, we don’t say ‘Ki Karan Deya’ like Majha flavor, we say ‘Ki Kar Rea Ya’. I don’t remember the specific location, but I have distinct memories of one morning traveling in that region and one could see the ‘Hilly’ fog and mountains could be seen too. (which is interesting because I have spent time in ‘Dry and Deserted’ Punjab aka Malwa too, though Punjab is usually famous for Green fields and plains). Over the years I have heard many Himachali Languages and Dogri. And naturally, the language of Una seems very closer to our speech. (Compared to other Pahadi vernaculars). My Older Brother told me he had a college friend from Una who spoke a language almost like Punjabi(mutually intelligible) and was speaking standard-type Punjabi within 2 months of living in Jalandhar. My Parents lived in Jammu for a few years as my Dad worked there on a Dam project. My Mother told me that Hindi had not penetrated much there yet(the early 80s) and many people didn’t speak Hindi, and while Punjabi and Dogri did have differences people were able to talk to each in their respective languages(mutually intelligible). Though Dogri has other differences, one thing similar between Doabi and Dogri is the usage of B instead of W/V of Majhi or Standard Punjabi for many words. For example, these words are spoken almost the same in Doabi and Dogri. Big - BaDDha - > बड्डा Also - Bi -> बी Twenty - Bih -> बीह् Hair - BaaL(Hair) -> बाल or बाळ Times - Baar(Times) -> बार Marriage - Biah -> ब्याह् To divide/distribute - BanD -> बंड Congrats - Badhayi -> बधाई , Basakhi instead of Vaisakhi and so on. I wrote these words from Google Translate of Dogri, while you won't find most of these in a ‘Standard’ Punjabi dictionary today. :) So, there are some distinct similarities in these adjoining vernaculars or dialect continuum regions, but otherwise, over the last 60–70 years, after the formation of Punjab State, the difference and separation are more solidified, which is bound to happen. Punjabi(Indian)/Doabi is in a healthy state today, we use Gurmukhi which is a living script, while the Kangri/Dogri script of Takri/Dogra Akkhar is almost extinct. Also, Himachal/Jammu uses Hindi as the official language unlike Punjab, so these native languages are declining at a faster rate. (as far as I am aware Dogri is not taught in Schools). It’s an ironic state of affairs because Dogra Akkhar had official state status before Gurmukhi. (during Kingdom times). I have put a Video link below in the comment section of a Dogri and Punjabi speaker interacting in Jammu in their respective languages. Image Courtesy : Google Images.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What does the Punjabi word 'Paaji' mean?
Answer: In Eastern Punjabi or at least the one I am aware of, Paaji is not a word per se. It's Bhaji. I call any older Male Cousin Bhaji and the younger ones call me Bhaji. I have learned that there are perhaps dialects or languages in the Greater Punjab region or say Delhi-influenced Punjabi which pronounce this ਭ Bhabha sound as P but on Eastern Side, it is intact as the Tonal Bh sound, which is different from the Hindi/Sanskrit or the Urdu/Persian sound of Bha(भ/بھ). You can see its usage in the following words, Bha - Cost, Ki Bha Laya (If you say Bha as Pa, it would mean ‘to put something in’). Bhalekha - Confusion BhaRta - A brinjal based dish BhaRak - A flare BhanDa - A utensil BhangRa - A dance form Bhua - Aunt, Father’s Sister Bhabi - Brothers Wife, also a Card Game. Bharat - The country of India And so one, dozens and hundreds of words. In none of them, do we pronounce this Bh as P. (Nor does Gurmukhi Punjabi dictionaries put them under the P sound). Now the thing is it’s not just limited to Bh but rather a whole slew of tonal sounds as shown below which belong to the same category,[1] That is why the Punjabi pronounciations for Home(Ghar), Milk(Dhudh), Lie(Jhuth), Lid(Dhakkan) are all different from Hindi/Urdu. So, I am interested to know if this Bh -> P , happens to other sounds too or not. When (घ झ ढ ध भ گھ جھ ڈھ دھ بھ) are used to write ਘ ਝ ਢ ਧ ਭ , they actually render Hindi/Sanskrit or Urdu/Persian sounds rather than Punjabi. It is because of the way these letters are pronounced in Punjabi, that kind of pronunciation is not present in any other language of India. And for transliteration, the equivalent or closest letters of Devanagari are used in the dictionary. For example, In this video skit, when the girl says Bhan Diyangi, it clearly is not the Punjabi Bh sound, thus it becomes obvious that a Hindi person is speaking Punjabi. Question: Do Punjabi and Bengali languages have any similarities in terms of their origins and development of words/phrases used by them?
Answer: Well, both are Indo-Aryan Languages so if you put the effort to break down the words, sentences, grammar, and loan words sure you can find some similarities. Like, (Punjabi-Bengali) When - Kadon - Kokhon Then - Tadon - Tokhon Here - Eithe - Eikhane Where - Kithe - Kothay There - Utthe - Uikhane (Will) Happen - Houga - Hobe. I mean if you do consider that similar, still if you hear them being spoken fast, most likely you will miss them. Lexical similarity is also on the low end, I would guess less than 50%. Grammar is also a bit different. Bengali seems to have little more usage of straight Sanskrit loanwords while modifying the sound, as LavaN(Salt) becomes Lobon in Bengali while Punjabi uses the Prakrit-derived version LooN. (I have learned there are parts of Bengal and Punjab where Noon/NooN is used instead). Vriksh(Tree) becomes Brikho in Bengali but Birkh in Punjabi.Though in normal speech we use Rukh/Darakht in Punjabi and Gaach in Bengali for Tree. The scripts also while derived from Brahmi are widely different due to geographical distance. This is my name written in Punjabi and Bengali ਕੰਵਲਪਾਲ ਸਿੰਘ ਫਲੋਰਾ (P) and কানওয়ালপাল সিং ফ্লোরা(B) In Bengali, we can’t write the W sound but we can write consonant clusters like the FL sound, but in Punjabi for the most part, F and L are separate sounds. The inherent vowel in Bengali is ‘O’ and in ‘A’ in Punjabi. Bengali doesn’t use much ‘S’ but rather ‘Sh’. All these make the languages pretty much Mutually Unintelligible.

Question: Is it hard to learn Punjabi?
Answer: There is nothing specifically hard in learning Punjabi. It's just like any other language. Of course, it has its own idiosyncracies with regard to accent, pronunciation, and colloquial usage as expected, but that can be learned as one goes along. Recently, I noted myself using the words: E’Che to say ‘in it’. It is actually Eh De Wich, when written in Punjabi and also if spoken in proper standard Punjabi. Or you hear, Saatoon , which is actually Saade Toon. (from Us). Gurmukhi also doesn't fully encompass many sounds or usages of Punjabi. The ‘h’ sound many times is not fully pronounced in Punjabi, like ‘Reha’ is Rea or Naha is N’ha to Bath, Seher(City) is S’her. Name is written as Naam but pronounced as ‘Naa’. Bimaar(Sick) is written as such but spoken as Bamaar. (first vowel weakens in many words). In written Punjabi, sentences end with ‘Hai’ but in spoken form almost never used and instead aa, ne, ya, ae etc are used. In all the above cases, if one speaks bookish Punjabi or how it is written, that is also fine and fully understood, and as I said one picks up these subtle things with time. (Infact Standard Punjabi should be used if one wants most Punjabis to understand). These can be seen as slang but most are not, it was done just in an effort to standardize the language. (spoken form already existed).

Question: What is the meaning of Vadh in Hindi?
Answer: Vadh, वध is a Sanskrit word meaning to Kill someone. Thus the word exists in Shuddh Hindi as same. Though, one would mostly hear the word used in Religious or Mythological TV series or Hindi Literature. In Street Language, I guess Marna or Qatal is usually used. In Standard Punjabi, Wadh (ਵਧ) has a different meaning as something has ‘increased’, which in Hindi is BaDh (बढ़). But interestingly, Punjabi has a depreciated or old usage for Wadh also, which our elders used to mention to us. For example, if you have a material possesion, like Money or Wheat and it has finished, we were told not to say Atta Muk Gaya or Atta Khatam Ho Gaya, but rather Atta Wadh Gaya. Or the usage was Wadha Pey Gaya. Here Wadh/Wadha actually means the things have finished/no longer exist, but are expressed as that they have increased. (because it would be unfortunate to state the obvious reality).

Question: Is it possible for a non-Punjabi speaker to speak fluent Punjabi in a short time (say, three months)?
Answer: The answer would be No. I know of only 1 Non-Punjabi, from Haridwar who learned how to speak Punjabi fluently. (There may have been more but my memory is failing me). It took him 4 years to live in a very rural Malwa region of Punjab and consistently use Punjabi as much as possible. Recently I talked to him and he said one of the reasons was that our cousin always talked back to him in Punjabi, other than his genuine interest to learn the Language. It's not like Hindi speakers/people from adjoining states who live/study/work in Punjab always start learning Punjabi. Some people out of interest may learn little Punjabi, but many others can just use Hindi. So, Hindi-speaking people will always have this challenge when learning Punjabi, because almost all Punjabis in Urban regions would already know Hindi/Urdu/English. In this said case while the Punjabi being spoken is fluent, one can still tell some Hindi effects in pronunciations, etc. Very many people who say it’s an easy and quick activity to learn both Punjabi and Hindi/Urdu will actually be Punjabis who have studied Hindi/Urdu in school. (That is in Urban Punjab they grew up in an almost Bilingual environment). I have written many answers but a quick summary if one only knows Hindi/Urdu wanting to learn Punjabi: 40% are totally new words, the other 50% the same root words but spoken in different forms or structure/tones, and only the last ~10% words give respite as they are same. To native speakers of Punjabi, its very easy to pick up the differences of pronunciation even if its subtle. Another example is the Bollywood Punjabi community of Mumbai/Delhi, whose newer generation has completely lost the capability to speak Punjabi, if Punjabi was easy for Hindi/Urdu speakers, then that would not have happened. And this example was from Hindi speaking area, if we go further away it will become even harder. A answer here from German prespective once mentioned 5–10 years to learn Punjabi. On his website, Writer Samir Chopra(a Punjabi), shares his life experiences of trying to learn Punjabi later in his life, [1] My progress in learning Punjabi was halting; all too often, in the midst of a conversation, my verbs, tenses and vocabulary would break down and I would have to, yet again, switch back to the safety of Hindi-Urdu. I discovered that the Punjabi spoken in the Punjabi hinterland–of whose representatives in New York City there were many–was far harder to master than the urban variant I had been previously exposed to, and I would frequently switch to Hindi-Urdu in the middle of a conversation, unable to keep up with the barrage of incomprehensible words coming my way.

Question: Is Punjabi a dialect of Saraiki/Multani?
Answer: They are languages of a shared region. It is said that the language we call Punjabi today was called Multani at some point. A Landa-based Brahmi script also existed to write Multani called Multani Script[1], belonging to the same family as Gurmukhi but it is extinct today. The first person (Baba Farid) who conferred or helped to give an Independent linguistic identity to the Punjabi Language was from Multan. I also recently saw a video of a Jatki Language speaker claiming that theirs is the real language or ‘sound’ of the Greater Punjab Region. Jatki is closer to Saraiki. Personally, I consider myself an Eastern Punjabi speaker.[2]We have some dialects here also but since the education and mass media is in a Standard form of Punjabi, the dialects will eventually phase out as usually happens. We also generally use the Gurmukhi script. So, I consider Saraiki a separate language. As mentioned there were historical links but there has been divergence along the way. I mean Eastern Punjab is already separated from Western Punjab, so we don't even have any reaction to Southern West Punjab or Saraiki movement, in fact all that already happened on the Eastern side in the 1950–60s with the reorganization of the current Indian Punjab. In the long history of languages, these things happen. Saraiki alphabet is still being developed based on Arabic Sindhi as it shares some sounds with Sindhi and the people of the Lower West Punjab region use Urdu officially and most people who moved to India from that region use Hindi as their language of education. (in regions like Haryana and Delhi). One time I interacted with a Sindhi from Upper Sindh who could speak Saraiki. I also tried to learn the ڳ (ģāf) sound which is little different from Eastern Punjabi. We use Gurmukhi to write Punjabi and use it as an official/literary Language(basically we were able to ‘secure’ the future of the language). I hope Saraiki People can also one day fully develop their Arabic-based Rasm-Ul-Khat like Sindhi and use Saraiki as a Official Language.

Question: My jaw just dropped when I heard about over 450 languages are spoken in India My question is, how much difference is there between Indo-arian languages and Dravidian languages? Are they somewhat similar or totally different?
Answer: Indo-Aryan(Northern) and Dravidian(Southern) are completely unintelligible. Indo-Aryan Standardized languages are as different or more than European National Languages. For example, Punjabi and Hindi(Bollywood) have around 60% Lexical Similarity compared to 82% of Spanish-Italian or 89% of Spanish-Portuguese. Very many times, on Punjabi youtube video comments, we can see Hindi speakers saying they can't understand what's being spoken. Of course, we have sub-regional dialects, for example, I speak the Doabi dialect of Punjabi, and I was born and grew up in the Rangpuri/Bahe dialect-speaking region of Bengal. Indo-Aryan Scripts like Punjabi, Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, and Odia are also different and mostly unintelligible. (though there are similarities) Dravidian/Southern Scripts of course are different again. The scripts unlike the Spoken form, do belong to the same Brahmi family (as do Javanese, Thai, Balinese etc). Easy way to visualize India would be like European Union(just with more scripts).

Question: My mother tongue Paudhi in Northern Haryana is dying due to the influence of Hindi. Can it survive in the upcoming years?
Answer: It is not an easy topic. I am not an expert but Paudhi Language or Dialect is a Continuum that is merged in the Paudh region between Punjab and Haryana. Though from my understanding bigger region falls in Punjab and around the villages of Chandigarh. The reason it may be hard for me to explain is that I grew up in a family who considered themselves ‘Punjabi’. We didn’t have a strong consciousness of a dialectal or sub-regional identity because we didnt grow up in North India/Punjab. We speak the Doabi dialect but it has the benefit of being popular in mass media, and also is part of a central-eastern region where Punjabi is used/taught officially. But we don’t speak like how Majhi or Malwai is spoken, though these differences are slowly diluting in Punjab due to standard education and intermixing. These dialects of Eastern Punjab are eventually going to die out or become really diluted as people merge into the ‘Punjabi’ or Eastern Punjabi identity. In Indian Punjab, linguistically Paudhi is considered a dialect of Punjabi, at times associated with the Malwa region. I am part of a couple of Reddit Punjabi subs and I see people who like to speak/promote their sub-regional vernacular and some don’t even like the usage of Standard Punjabi(because doing so may eventually submerge or consume their dialect), so I understand these sentiments. I am also aware that there are other hierarchical dynamics people get involved in ie which are more prestigious dialects, which are rural and urban speech etc, but since we didn’t grow up in North India/Punjab, we escaped it completely. So, you have to answer the question for yourself. Do you consider Paudhi closer or part of the greater Punjabi Language. Then you can learn Punjabi/Paudhi in Gurmukhi script. If not, that is also fine, you can research Paudhi words/speech and maybe make a booklet or dictionary with Paudhi -> Punjabi or Paudhi -> Hindi translation for coming generations to refer to. That will be your contribution to your mother tongue. But if it makes you feel a little better, eventually all languages and even our Earth is going to die, just that some will last longer than others :). So, if Paudhi dies, one day Punjabi, Hindi, and English will also die.

Question: What scripts of modern India descended from the Sarada script?

North/North-West historical Indian region had Sarada derived native scripts like Takri, Dogra Akkhar, Khudabadi, Mahajani, Multani, Khojki and Gurmukhi. All of these are called ‘Lande’ scripts. Most of these regions use Devanagari/Perso-Arabic scripts and Hindi/Urdu as official languages today except Indian Punjab. (Gorkhaland Territorial Administration) Hindi/Urdu : Even though the region doesn’t really have Hindi-Hinterland presence(apart from perhaps in the Army camps/students), Hindi is present there as ‘Trade’ or ‘Link’ language. Also is taught in central schools. My Dad and one uncle are especially big fans of Mohd Rafi. Punjabi : We continue to talk in Punjabi as our Native/Mother tongue, one with a Doabi touch. My Dad also worked in places like Silchar in Assam too. I also have experienced many of these linguistic flavors but in most cases I am weaker than my Dad because I left Bengal at age 15. Or rather I should say Northern Bengal/Dooars/Foothills of the Himalayas as the region is really diverse linguistically. The region was already at the cross roads due to proximity to Nepal/Bhutan and tiny corridor joining the North East with Mainland India, but the British really relished living there during Summers as their abode, which coupled with their love for Tea eventually led to the influx of trade/worker communities in the region at their behest in the 19th and early 20th century, and finally the Bengal Partition/Bangladesh freedom added to the diversity of the region. Question: Do Hindi and Punjabi speakers have difficulty understanding each other?
Answer: Modern Hindi/Urdu and Punjabi have around 60% Lexical Similarity, which actually make them pretty different languages (more different than say Spanish vs Italian which have 82% lexical similarity), but most Urban Punjabis know Hindi/Urdu because of education, mass media and the fact that Hindustani has been the lingua franca/official language of Northern India/Greater Punjab region for 175+ years now. Hindi is taught in Rural Punjab also, my Mother studied Hindi in a remote Punjab village in the 60’s. In a recent survey, Maharashtra and Punjab were the top most Hindi friendly Non-Hindi states. Infact, some of the most prominent works in Hindustani Language of last 100 years have been done by Punjabis (Urdu Literature and Bollywood etc). My Dad’s favorite Urdu/Hindustani singer is Mohd Rafi who was a Punjabi. He is also regarded by many as the top Urdu singer of Bollywood. As we move away from Punjab towards Delhi, Hindi speakers may understand some Punjabi, but by the time we hit the Central India, I doubt a Hindi speaker can understand much of Punjabi. This hierarchical relationship is common in Regional Language vs Lingua Franca dynamics. Regional people know the lingua franca more than vice-versa. I have a Aunt from Punjabi Background who grew up in Rajasthan. She cant Speak Punjabi, her Daughter has in recent years started to learn Punjabi. My Paternal Grandmother studied both Punjabi and Urdu in her childhood(in Sargodha) but forgot how to read Urdu and could never speak Urdu, only spoke Punjabi. She had created a hybrid kind of language(based on Punjabi :)) mixing all languages She got exposed to since age 20 or so, when she left Punjab, that was the language she spoke with Non-Punjabis. (our neighbors were Marwari and Bengali). That also shows that if people live long enough together they can interact with each other even if they don’t really know each other’s respective languages, one just needs to have some patience. Infact that’s how creoles or pidgins are created. But this is not a norm or standard phenomenon, it’s a necessity of life kind of thing. To answer the question, usually there is no difficulty, because Punjabis can almost always interact in Hindi/Urdu(in varying degrees). Sure you can find some Punjabi monolinguals like my Grandmother if you try but that would become a rarer trend in times to come.

Question: What is RF test engineering?
Answer: RF Engineering is a branch of Electrical Engineering. We can call it a specialization. RF Engineering can be split between RF Design and RF Test. I am a RF Test Engineer. RF stands for Radio Frequency. The first company I worked for, was Meggitt Defense Systems(earlier Cartwright Electronics), which recently got bought by Parker. We worked on Radar Systems. Radars can find the distance and speed of an moving object. With multi-antenna vector systems they can even make a ‘signature’ ie rough shape of the object. Yes, they can see the object but just in a little different way than light rays. SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) is an application of imaging the targets/objects. I worked there for almost 6.5 years. The opening lines of Scitech classic Introduction to Airborne Radar by Smitson explains the phenomenon.[1] Tapping the sidewalk repeatedly with his cane, a blind man makes his way along a busy street, keeping a fixed distance from the wall of a building on his right—hence also a safe distance from the curb and the traffic whizzing by on his left. Emitting a train of shrill beeps, a bat deftly avoids the obstacles in its path and unerringly homes in on a succession of tiny nocturnal insects that are its prey. And ofcourse with RF comes Antenna’s which are described as : An antenna is a device for accomplishing a transition between a guided electromagnetic wave and a wave which propagates in free space. [2] Over the last 8+ years I have been working at Panasonic Avionics. We make Antenna Systems (Bi-directional and Active ie having gains on both TX/RX paths), used for Wifi in Aeroplanes. They are installed on the top of the Aeroplane under a Radome(Radar-Dome) and communicate with Satellite Systems through the free space, which communicate back to Earth Stations to complete the link. There are specialized RF Test Equipment's like Spectrum Analyzer, Vector Network Analyzer, Vector Signal Analyzer, Phase Noise/Noise Figure testers, Power Meters and many more. Antennas are tested both in open air (Far Field) and in Enclosed spaces called Anechoic Chambers which use many techniques to shrink the space needed to form plane wavefronts and still get good radiation patterns. There are many RF Design Softwares also, both for PCB design and System Simulation. I used a Software called Systemvue during my Masters Thesis, which can do a full RF system simulation.[3] Hopefully, this gives some idea about RF Engineering.

Question: Why does Quora not have Punjabi and Urdu languages?

Gurmukhi(which is the only official/literary script for Punjabi today) is accessible to around 27 million Punjabis but even within India, it is not really a fully unifying script for Punjabi(large number of Punjabis living outside Indian Punjab, who may know Punjabi verbally usually don’t know Gurmukhi). Question: Why is Punjabi considered a separate language when it is 80%-90% similar to Hindi/Urdu?
Answer: Punjabi is not that similar to Hindi/Urdu at all. Just above half of the lexical root is shared. And the rest half are totally new and separate words. For example Spanish and Portuguese are said to have 89% Lexical Similarity while its only 58-61% between Punjabi and Hindi/Urdu. That means we can and do create/speak entire sentences in Punjabi where almost all of the words are different from Hindi/Urdu. Even the words which may have shared ancestral root have deviated so much that to an un-trained ear they might seem as different words. Jisne -> Jenhe , Aati -> Aundi or Jahan/Kahan -> Jitthe/Kitthe not to mention other pronunciation differences like tones and geminations which are present more in Punjabi, eg Aik -> Ekk, Laat -> Latt, Aakh -> Akkh. In actuality, the number of words which are exactly same in Punjabi and Hindi/Urdu may be as low as 10% or even less. Also there are few situations where words which are similar/same in meaning are used differently in context, for example , ‘don't throw this’ in Punjabi is ‘Eh Sutti Naa’ , in Hindi/Urdu is ‘Yeh Fekna Mat’. Now , ‘Naa’ for No is also a word in Hindi but here it is not used. While ‘theoretically’ Grammar is similar, the way words are modified and twists like above make it not so straight forward process for acquiring intelligibility. ‘Sleep’ in Hindi is Sona (सोना), and in Punjabi it is SauNa (सौणा). But when saying ‘to sleep’, it becomes SauN Layi (सौंण लइी) in Punjabi, where the equivalent of Ke, ie De can be and is dropped as in Hindi it is , Sone Ke Liye (सोने के लिए). The ke is mandatory here, along with the obvious change in the Vowels of both word. The reverse of this also happens. A Hindi speaking person trying to grasp Punjabi will be thrown off by things like these also, not to mention 40–50% completely new vocabulary He or She has to learn before mastering Punjabi. Now, investigating about Spanish and Portuguese one can find out that they are also pretty different languages having distinct sounds, so Hindi/Urdu and Punjabi are even further apart. I found this anecdote by an British officer in an article[1] about the time when British were trying to introduce Hindustani(Urdu) in Punjab in the mid 19th century, Even after almost 175 years, you can find videos of rural Punjab where students are being taught, English -> Urdu -> Punjabi, to make them understand the meaning of the words.

Question: What does ''ਕਰਨ' mean in Punjabi?

But the source root of ਕਰਨ or Karan exists in 2 more Punjabi words today which were derived from it. The source can be traced to both word Karṇa (कर्ण) and करोति Karoti in Sanskrit. Thus it lends to 2 words , one is Ear and other the act of doing something. First Karna for Ear has become ‘Kann’ ਕੰਨ in Punjabi. Second Karoti becomes Kamm, ਕੱਮ, ie the work done.

Question: Why do people call Lahore as Lohar instead of Lahore?
Answer: The Punjabi spelling of Lahore is لہور. Lhor/Lhore. In Gurmukhi it can be written as ਲਹੌਰ. Thing is we can write it as Lhore and Lahore also but regardless of how it is written in spoken Punjabi the first syllable is invariably subdued as the second syllable is stressed, so this sound is a property of Punjabi language. It is noted here, [1] This heavy stress pattern also naturally affects the shape of numerous Persian loanwords (here transcribed in Indo-Persian form with the vowels a ā i ī u ū ē ai ō au)in all varieties of Punjabi, in which heavy stress upon the second syllable causes weakening of the first, e.g. ka’tāb (< ketāb) “book,” ha’kūmat (<ḥokumat)“government’, a’vāz (< āvāz)“voice,” a’sānī (<āsāni)“ease,” ru’māl (< rūmāl)“handkerchief.” Other example I can remember is ‘Sick’ is written as Bimaar but pronounced as -> Bamaar. It is further exaggerated in the word ਲਹੌਰੀਆ, Lahoriya ie someone belonging to Lahore, as it almost sounds like Looriya or Lhooriya. Thing is the ہ/ਹ when occurring in the middle of a word in Punjabi accompanied with a vowel, leads to a variety of sounds. For example, ‘Many’ is written as Bahut but pronounced as Baut, ‘Beautiful’ Sohna becomes Sona. ‘Father in Law’, Sahura becomes Saura and so on. As historically Lahore is a Punjabi city, these are all correct pronunciations, with people calling it as they have been for centuries. In Hindustani/Urdu language which is the Official Language of Lahore, it is pronounced as لاہور, with uniform stress. Many Indic scripts have the half vowel inbuilt in the abiguda, while in Latin script at times it’s hard to decipher the proper pronunciation of the said vowel when trying to write Indo-Aryan languages.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: Could you give a written example of how your dialect differs from standard pronunciation?
Answer: 'Doabi' Punjabi is not hugely different from Standard Indian Punjabi as some other dialects of Punjabi are. My Paternal side, though born outside Punjab is mostly from Jalandhar area and Maternal side from Hoshiarpur. As per my Mother, in really old times people didn’t mingle much or have relationships outside their region of what are called Up-Bhasha/Lehja or Dialects today, due to similarity of habits/culture within their respective region. Inter migration thus is a relatively new phenomenon with advancement in transportation. Honestly, for the most part listening to Doabi type Punjabi is the norm in Punjabi Mass Media today, probably because most Newspapers/Media and DD Punjabi is in Jalandhar plus early NRI media and songs came from the Doaba region, so they seem neutral and familiar to us. The Leading Punjabi newspaper in USA is Desh Doaba. Official status also plays a role I believe and has benefited it, as Doabi falls in region of Punjab where Punjabi is used as official language, so as Doaba region has played a big role in mainstream representation of Modern Punjabi language its just a natural experience to hear it.[1] I have written few dozen pages in using Standard Punjabi, so some differences I can think of currently are: Standard Punjabi = Doabi Punjabi. Han = Ya Haan/Hai = Ya/Aa San = Sigey/Si Kiven = Kiddan Jiven = Jiddan Eiven = Eiddan Vekho = Dekho Usage of B/Bh instead of V/W(though at times it’s a soft B/Bh sound). Waal = Baal(Hair) Vaar = Baar(Times) Vi = Bhi(Also) Viah = Biah(Marriage) Wadda = Bhadda(Big) Wich = Bech(Inside) Vohti = Bhoti(Wife) Wadd = Bhadd(To cut/separate) WanD = BanD(to distribute) Vaisakhi = Basakhi(Festival) Wadhayi = Badhayi (Congrats) Some of these Doabi words you can’t find in dictionary so you use the standard Punjabi equivalents. But it’s not like we can’t speak V/W sound or don’t use it, we do in many words like Wadhiya(Good), Wall(Towards), Wang(Type), Wakh(separate). Sentence example: In Standard Punjabi if we write, ‘How are you?’, it is : Tussi Kiven Ho? But when will speak Doabi Punjabi it more like : Tussi Kiddan Haige Ya? Ofcourse there is lots of regional vocabulary and Aakhan too, like Ghabbe(In between) rather than Vichkaar, Dhaun instead of Gardan(Neck), Niana(kid) and very many others. So, while there are indeed differences, it was not a huge leap for someone like me to start writing in Bookish/Standard Punjabi even if all of our knowledge is verbal based for the most part along with living outside Punjab for long time. I lived for a few years in Malwa region and with Majha region students, so we just know so many of each other words and sayings due to this intermixing nowadays. Actually what I do is, I check the dictionary/grammar to make sure what I am writing is covered in Dictionary and as long as it is, then I don't need to change it. So, the parts of Doabi which have already been incorporated into Standard Punjabi, I can just use as such, thus eventually it comes out as Standard+Doabi, though Standard Punjabi takes precedence. You can check grammar of a written line also in Akkhar Software, and for the most part grammar is very similar between Doabi and Standard Punjabi. If you have heard Mickey Singh, I can say we mostly speak like him, as he is also from Hoshiarpur/Jalandhar area. So, this type of song or media is very normal and near to our language.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What is Yak called in Punjabi?
Answer: Yak(Bos grunniens) is a Domesticated Cattle found in the Tibetan region and the foothills of the Himalayas/Nepal, and other Mountainous/Hilly regions.[1][2] It has particularly hairy body hair, to survive the harsh winters and cold climates of the regions. Its Milk is edible and widely used in both liquid and dried from. The Hair is used for Dresses/Costumes. The dung for energy and Bulls are used for carrying loads and weights in the hilly regions. Since its a foreign word to the Punjab region, we can refer to it in few different ways. ਤਿੱਬਤੀ ਗਾਂ : Tibbati Gaan, the Cow from Tibet. ਤਿੱਬਤ ਅਤੇ ਹਿਮਾਲਾ ਦੇ ਖੇਤਰਾਂ ਵਿਚ ਮਿਲਨ ਵਾਲੀ ਲੰਮੇ ਅਤੇ ਰੇਸ਼ਮੀ ਵਾਲਾਂ ਵਾਲੀ ਗਾਂ : Tibbat ate Himala De Khetera Wich Milan Wali Lamme ate Reshmi Walan Wali Gaan. (The cow from Tibet and Himalaya regions which has long and silky hairs). ਸੁਰ ਗਾਂ : Sur Gaan. ਯਾਕ : Just ‘Yak’ The Animal does have an interesting link with Punjabi people(actually Sikhs). The Guru Granth Sahib is flanked by a hand made fan(a fly whisk), which is called ‘Chaur Sahib’. [3] ਚੌਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. It is actually made of Yak Tail Hair and retains its shine even after years of usage.[4] Since we grew up in region where Yak products were available and used, we knew of this connection from childhood. This tradition was also used with the Gurus and is now used with the Sri Guru Granth Sahib. It was also a tradition used for kings and royalty. The use of the hair from a yak's tail was one of the royal symbols of Ghengis Khan the distant ancestor of Babur and the Mughals who despite being the rulers of 'Hindustan' long dreamed of retaking their forefather's homelands in the northern stepps. (In this case the grass was actually greener). चौँरी गाई, Chauri Gai is a Nepali name of a very similar Animal which is a mix of Yak and Domestic Cattle.(Tibetan Dzo)[5] Punjabi language thus also has a word Chaura(ਚੌਰਾ), for a Bullock which has short hairy tail like a Yak. Yet another personal anecdote I can share is how a special type of Hardened Cheese is made from Yak Milk, called Chhurpe in Nepali Language. Nepali: छुर्पी, Tibetan: ཆུར་བ། We used to eat it as Kids and its extra-ordinarily hard and you just keep in mouth and slowly suck/eat it over a long period of time.[6] [7] Its made by boiling the fermented Yak milk(buttermilk) and is very famous in the whole hilly region. The Mongols also have the similar milk products as they live in these extreme climates, and preparing food in such way leads to longer periods of preservation.

Name: Kanwalpal Singh Flora
Question: What is the meaning of Punjabi word 'Pind'?
Answer: ‘PinD’ ਪਿੰਡ in Punjabi means Village. Or in contextual terms it may also mean ‘Ancestral Region’, Jaddi Khetar , ਜੱਦੀ ਖੇਤਰ. For example, my Grandmother used to call the whole of Punjab region as ‘PinD’. She used to call Punjab as PinD, while living in India itself, as She was born in Sargodha and then left Punjab at early age for Bengal, and this reference continued when She lived in USA too. Second meaning in Punjabi for PinD ਪਿੰਡ is ‘Body’, also used is the word extension PinDa/ਪਿੰਡਾ. But I had been in search for root meaning for another PinD also and see if that was also a word in Punjabi. That quest has been since I learned the word for ‘Almsround’ for Buddhist Monks, is called Piṇḍapāta (पिण्डपात) in Pali. It’s the same word in Sanskrit too. Buddhist Monks go for morning Almsround ie food in their bowls, for their only meal for the day.[1] Piṇḍapāta (“food being offered to the Bhikkhus (pinda); bowl (pata)”).[2] In old times the food could have been just a ball of rice or meat. And in Punjabi dictionaries we can indeed find PinD also meaning ‘a ball of rice or barley or meat.’[3] They also refer to dried salted dates and mentioned in the song which goes a follows: LuNi PinD Da KihaN Sawad Hai, Andaren Di Wairi, Gaman Yar, Iho Dangaren Da Khaj Hai. ਲੂਣੀ ਪਿੰਡ ਦਾ ਕਿਹਣ ਸਵਾਦ ਹੈ, ਆਂਦਰਾਂ ਦੀ ਵੈਰੀ, ਗ਼ਮਾਂ ਯਾਰ, ਇਹੋ ਡੰਗਰਾਂ ਦਾ ਖਾਜ ਹੈ। لونی پنڈ دا کہن سواد ہے، آندراں دی ویری، غماں یار، ایہو ڈنگراں دا کھاج ہے۔ लूणी पिण्ड दा किहण सवाद है, आंदरां दी वैरी, ग़मां यार , इहो डंगरां दा खाज है। What flavor have salted dates? Gaman love, they are an enemy to the stomach-fit food for cattle only. So, this PinD(ਪਿੰਡ/पिण्ड) also has a different meaning in Old Punjabi/Prakrit and can be found in other Liturgical languages of Northern India ie Pali and Sanskirt.

Question: What is Pyo in Punjabi?
Answer: ਪਿਓ , Pyo is a particular Punjabi word for ‘Father’. It’s still in usage, but in modern times, it seems like it has been reserved to terms like Ma-Pyo(Mother/Father). or like the video below, Pyo Dhi Da Pyar, It’s rarely used by itself to address Dad or Father, and mostly used in 3rd person. Another related word in Punjabi is Peka or Peke, ਪੇਕਾ/ਪੇਕੇ, which means Parental House or Village/Town. If anyone has a deeper knowledge of the word or history of its usage, please share.
